@@122004686 <p> A new Massachusetts Institute of Technology-led study confirms that the Antarctic ozone layer is healing as a direct result of global efforts to reduce ozone-depleting substances . <p> Our planet 's natural ozone layer is the earth 's version of 50+ sunscreen -- its presence reduces UV and its carcinogenic effects . Complex life could not exist on this planet without the ozone layer . <p> But from early last century we started pouring refrigerants such as chlorofluorocarbons ( CFCs ) into the atmosphere . In 1986 studies revealed a " hole " over Antarctica , with evidence suggesting CFCs were to blame -- destroying ozone ( O3 ) faster than it could be naturally replenished , and reducing its protective effects . <p> Which lead to a global CFC ban in 1992 , known as the Montreal Protocol . <p> Watch NOAA 's animation of the daily progression through the 2024 season ( Above ) . The purple and blue colours are where there is the least ozone , and the yellows and reds are where there is more ozone . <p> Since then , the hole has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this was due to the reductions in ozone-depleting chemicals ; natural weather variability ; or increased greenhouse gas emissions in the stratosphere . <p> The Antarctic hole was relatively small during 2024 's peak depletion season -- September 7th to October 13th -- compared to other years , says NOAA . Small is relative -- it was still 22.4 million square kilometres , 3 times the size of Australia . <p> Now MIT researchers have added granularity and a little optimism to that prediction . <p> Coauthor Professor Susan Solomon of Environmental Studies and Chemistry at the MIT , and colleagues , noticed significant ozone hole recovery in 2016 . The hole seemed to be shrinking each year , she says . Solomon was part of the original research team that gave evidence of CFC harms that lead to the Montreal Protocol . <p> But why was the hole shrinking ? Was it CFCs , or was it weather variability from El Nino , La Nina or the polar vortex ? <p> " While detecting a statistically significant increase is relatively straightforward , attributing these changes to specific forcings is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ study , Peidong Wang , of the MIT 's Department of Earth , Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences . <h> Fingerprinting the ozone evidence <p> To resolve this question the MIT team borrowed a ' fingerprinting ' technique used by the climate change community to isolate specific climate factors from natural meteorological " noise " -- in this case attempting to remove the static from the CFC reduction-ozone hole recovery argument . <p> " The atmosphere has really chaotic variability within it , " Solomon says . " What we 're trying to detect is the emerging signal of ozone recovery against that kind of variability , which also occurs in the stratosphere . " <p> Computer model simulations were run with ' parallel worlds ' generated using the same global atmosphere with different starting conditions , say without greenhouse gases ( GHGs ) or CFCs , to isolate natural weather variability . Or with or without GHGs or CFCs to determine possible effects of both . Questions included how ozone changed with altitude and season , and with different starting conditions . From these simulations they mapped out times and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- a fingerprint showing that ozone recovery was due to declining ozone- depleting chemicals . In the model , at least . <p> So , they knew what to look for , but did this fingerprint appear in the real world ? Fifteen years of observational data on the Antarctic ozone hole were mined for this telltale sign . They saw it , becoming clearer and clearer , peaking in 2018 . <p> " After 15 years of observational records , we see this signal to noise with 95 percent confidence , suggesting there 's only a very small chance that the observed pattern similarity can be explained by variability noise , " Wang says . " This gives us confidence in the fingerprint . <p> " It also gives us confidence that we can solve environmental problems . What we can learn from ozone studies is how different countries can swiftly follow these treaties to decrease emissions . " <p> Solomon says there will soon be a year when the ozone layer stays entirely intact , here and there , and eventually shuts for good . <p> " By @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there 's no ozone hole depletion at all in the Antarctic . And that will be very exciting for me , " she says . " And some of you will see the ozone hole go away completely in your lifetimes . And people did that . " 
@@122004930 <p> With electricity prices shaping up to be a hot-button issue at the upcoming federal election , the Coalition has claimed we 're paying some of the world 's most expensive electricity bills , but experts say global comparisons are complicated . <p> Both Opposition Leader Peter Dutton and energy spokesperson Ted O'Brien have made the claim while taking aim at Labor 's future energy plans . When asked for evidence , Dutton 's office pointed to a comparison of prices -- what some people in South Australia pay against Canadians in Ontario and Americans in Tennessee , both of which have nuclear as part of their energy mix . <h> Are our electricity bills really among the world 's most expensive ? <p> Experts AAP FactCheck spoke to gave varying levels of credit to the Coalition 's claim , but they agreed on one thing : international comparisons of electricity prices are highly problematic . For a start , there 's a lack of quality in data sources . <p> Tony Irwin , a nuclear power expert from Australian National University , pointed to a 2021 comparison carried out @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It ranked Australia 88th most expensive of 230 countries . <p> Tony Wood , director of the Energy and Climate Change Program at Grattan Institute , pointed to data on Statista which takes its figures from the website Global Petrol Prices . For the most recent period ( three months to June 2024 ) , Australia was ranked 26th most expensive out of 148 . <p> However , both said such global comparisons mean very little . Instead , countries should be compared with those with similarly developed economies . <p> When looking at OECD countries , Australia sits 15th most expensive out of 38 countries for household electricity , according to Global Petrol Prices . A comparison made across 29 similar economies by insurance company Compare The Market puts Australia at 13th most expensive , based on December 2023 data . <p> But even comparing similarly developed economies is problematic , the experts say . <p> Bruce Mountain , director of the Victoria Energy Policy Centre , explained there are various costs that make up the price consumers pay for electricity . As well as the usage cost @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not include various taxes , distribution charges , network charges and subsidies . <p> Tristan Edis helped establish the energy research program at the Grattan Institute and is now a director at Green Energy Markets . He said certain costs included in the final bill can make such comparisons misleading , particularly when used to make the case for certain energy production sources . <p> In Australia and many parts of Europe , a number of taxes are often added to electricity supply , but Japan and Korea have lower levels of tax on electricity , he said . As a result , you 're often left " comparing apples with oranges or apples with bananas " , he said . <p> Edis also pointed to Australia 's high distribution charges and said there 's a very high cost to reach some remote regions , which is reflected in everyone 's power bills , regardless of location . <p> Associate Professor Irwin said Australia 's size also makes such comparisons difficult , given that the prices paid by some in South Australia , which has the most expensive bills in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Other experts pointed to wholesale electricity price -- at which it 's bought and sold in bulk before reaching consumers -- as a better way to gauge the price of energy production , before extras are added to bills . <p> Australia is the ninth cheapest ( at the time of writing ) when it comes to wholesale prices out of the 31 OECD countries tracked by the International Energy Agency . <p> Wood said wholesale prices can be useful for comparison , depending on what you 're trying to establish . <p> " Wholesale prices are ... highly dependent on the energy sources , the natural resources of the country , and on the nature of any wholesale market , " he said . <p> Transmission and distribution , Wood said , will be highly dependent on a country 's size and where people live . <p> " The costs will be bigger in a country with smaller populations and longer distances , " he said . <p> " You have to pull these figures apart to decide how much of any differences is down to physical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " <h> So where does that leave the Coalition 's claim ? <p> Acknowledging the difficulties of such a comparison , Mountain said it 's about right to say we pay " among " the highest bills in the world . <p> Irwin said the claim is true enough for those living in South Australia , while the average Australian is paying " nearer to the most expensive developed countries than the least expensive " . <p> While international comparisons are problematic , Mountain said they can offer a better understanding of the factors that affect electricity prices . <p> " It 's understandable that electricity prices can become a tool in political discourse , " he said , " not unreasonably considering their importance to consumers . <p> " Critical thinking and a discerning mindset are incumbent on listeners when political actors make claims about electricity prices . " <p> This article is republished from AAP FactCheck . <p> Have something to say about this article ? Write to us at letters@crikey.com.au . After the film 's premiere , one of America 's best-known critics proclaimed it a masterpiece for the ages . @@122053446 <h> Five Reasons You Might Qualify for Lower Car Insurance Premiums <p> Like homeowners insurance , auto insurance is getting significantly more expensive : Data show that policy costs rose 11% last year , likely due to factors like climate change , rising accident rates , and higher repair costs . Under certain circumstances , you may be able to offset or at least keep your car insurance premium stable , if not reduce it . <p> If you go through any of the following life changes , it may be time to call your insurance company about lowering your policy premium . <h> You 've moved <p> A move is a major life transition -- and one that could impact your auto insurance policy for the better in a few ways . First , insurers factor where you park your car into your rate , so living in a lower density or safer neighborhood can potentially save you some money . Moving also gives you the chance to bundle your renters or homeowners insurance policy with your auto policy if you have n't already , which typically reduces the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ driving habits , which we 'll get into next . <h> You 're driving less <p> Let 's say your move has put your closer to work , or you 've changed jobs or begun working remotely more frequently , or another shift in your routine has cut the number of miles you drive on a regular basis . Insurance companies consider annual mileage when calculating premiums , so a significant drop could save you some money . <h> Your family size has changed <p> If you 've had a teenager on your policy who now has their own vehicle or own policy and no longer lives at home , removing them from yours can save you a significant amount of money on your premiums ( potentially cutting the cost by half ) . On the flip side , combining your policy with a new spouse 's could reduce the cost per person . <h> Your coverage is about to renew ( or expire ) <p> Re-upping your policy wo n't save you money specifically , but it is a good time to call your current insurer about options for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cheaper options . <h> Other ways to lower your car insurance premium <p> Even if you do n't have a life change that could qualify you for a lower insurance premium , there are other ways to reduce the cost of your policy : <p> Increase your deductible : Raising your deductible ( the amount you 'll pay out of pocket before your policy kicks in ) can lower your premium . Most policies have a $500 deductible , but bumping that up to $1,000 can potentially save you 25% on your policy cost , according to Consumer Reports . However , you 'll want to consider whether you have an emergency fund to cover the added potential cost . <p> Decrease certain types of coverage : Collision and comprehensive coverage may be optional in your state , and dropping one or both can reduce your policy premium . @@122103448 <h> Hugh White Trump 's conduct on Ukraine prompts strategic reckoning <p> This week , Prime Minister Anthony Albanese reassured us he has complete faith in America 's security guarantee . That is not a big surprise . In recent years , as China has challenged the familiar and agreeable American-led order in Asia , both sides of politics have lazily assumed we could depend on the United States to defend that order . The Europeans have done the same as Russia 's challenge to the post-Cold War European order has grown . They have assumed they could rely on the US to keep Russia at bay and preserve the status quo . <p> Today , thanks to US President Donald Trump , the Europeans know beyond a shadow of a doubt they were wrong . Now they face their gravest strategic reckoning in generations . Far from being defeated in Ukraine , Russia looks poised for a win that delivers most of what it wanted and leaves Europe vulnerable to whatever Trump might do next . <p> Before we rush to offer Europe our modest assistance in dealing with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we might want to pause to consider what we can learn from Europe 's predicament . There is a lot to learn , because the Europeans are themselves to blame for much of the mess in which they now find themselves . <p> Nothing , of course , can excuse Trump 's conduct , and not just that deplorable scene in the Oval Office last Friday . He is not only failing to support Ukraine , he is also actively helping Russia . We should be shocked by this , but we can hardly be surprised . No one can say Trump did n't tell us . <p> The Europeans did n't take Trump seriously . They ignored anything that contradicted the orthodox vision of a world happily prospering under US leadership , and with American power always on hand to deal swiftly with any recalcitrants -- including Russia . <p> It has become increasingly clear that Ukraine , fighting by itself , could not liberate its territory and inflict on Moscow a devastating defeat . That was what America and its European allies once insisted was essential if Putin @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is now almost 20 years since Russian President Vladimir Putin , in a famous speech in Munich , announced his determination to defy this vision and restore Russia 's place as a great power . This was n't just talk . He invaded Georgia in 2008 and seized chunks of Ukraine in 2014 , including Crimea , before launching a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 . The Europeans believed Washington 's foreign policy establishment -- everyone except Trump -- when they assured them that the US would take the lead and fix it . After all , had n't America always been there ? <p> What the Europeans overlooked was how much the strategic fundamentals have changed . The US committed itself to defend Europe from Russia when Europe was too weak to defend itself and Russia -- then the Soviet Union -- looked strong enough to dominate Eurasia and threaten the US itself . That gave America no choice but to carry the immense cost and risks of Europe 's defence . <p> Since the Cold War , everything has been different . Russia is much weaker and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stronger . Europe has the population , economy and technology base of a truly formidable power , and could easily defend itself from Russia without help from the US . In these circumstances , it has made no strategic sense for America to do the defending instead . <p> It suited key players on both sides of the Atlantic to pretend otherwise , however . American foreign policy types liked to bask in the glow of global leadership and pose as Europe 's guardians , while the Europeans got addicted to relying on the US rather than defending themselves . Both sides nurtured the illusion that the US 's strategic commitment to Europe was ironclad . <p> Russia 's full-scale invasion of Ukraine destroyed that illusion long before Donald Trump was re-elected . Indeed , the decisive moment came even before the invasion , when then US president Joe Biden pre-emptively declared that under no circumstances would American forces be sent to fight in Ukraine . His excuse was that Ukraine was not in NATO , but that was not the point . He himself proclaimed that Russia 's complete @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ survival of the global order . This was not a fight that the US could dodge and still pose as Europe 's defender . <p> The real reason Biden would not fight for Ukraine was Russia 's nuclear weapons . Biden feared that any battles between US and Russian forces in Ukraine could too easily escalate into a full-scale nuclear World War III . Events justified Biden 's nuclear fears , and there was one moment when the threat of nuclear war looked all too real . <p> That was in September and October 2022 , when successful Ukrainian counteroffensives seemed poised to drive Russian forces out of Ukraine altogether . Washington thought there was a 50 per cent chance Russia would use tactical nuclear weapons to stop them . If they did , US policymakers struggled to imagine an adequate response that would not risk a full-scale nuclear war . Biden was clear that Ukraine , and Europe , and the global order , was n't worth that . The Europeans followed Washington 's lead and stayed out of the fight . They did n't want to confront a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ seem to matter . The Europeans and Americans convinced themselves that Ukraine did n't need other countries to go into battle alongside them . Ukraine 's spectacular early victories , including the defence of Kyiv and the brilliant counteroffensives in late 2022 , made it seem credible that the Ukrainians could decisively defeat Russia and reclaim all their territory without direct combat help from the US and its allies . All the latter needed to do was provide Ukraine with weapons and money and the Ukrainians themselves could do all the fighting . <p> This was an illusion . That became clear in the middle of 2023 , when Ukraine 's much-hyped summer offensives mostly failed to materialise , and those that were launched broke on Russia 's well-prepared defences . Since then , as the war has dragged on , it has become increasingly clear that Ukraine , fighting by itself , could not liberate its territory and inflict on Moscow a devastating defeat . That was what the US and its European allies once insisted was essential if Putin 's great-power ambitions were to be crushed and Europe @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Americans and Europeans have backed off . Rather than join the fight themselves , over the past year they have slowly and stealthily come to accept that Russia will not be defeated . Instead , they realise Ukraine must make a peace that leaves Russia occupying a lot of Ukrainian territory , locks Ukraine out of NATO and leaves it vulnerable to Putin 's next move . <p> This was the situation when Trump took office . By siding with Russia and , it seems , deliberately humiliating President Volodymyr Zelensky for his own gratification , Trump has made an already tragic situation much worse . Before , the Europeans might have hoped to keep working with Washington to help ameliorate Ukraine 's appalling predicament . Not anymore . <p> Worse , from the Europeans ' point of view , they now face the task of containing Russia without America 's help . They have the power to do so , but they lack the political organisation , and they do n't have much time to summon it . Once they have done that , they face a truly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forces to Ukraine , ready and able to fight to deter or defeat any further Russian attacks -- or , if they will not defend what is left of Ukraine , they decide where they will draw the line against Russia 's ambitions . <p> It is not a new problem : ever since Peter the Great made Russia a European great power , the rest of Europe has had to decide how far west it should be allowed to spread . Wherever they draw the line this time , they will have to be willing to defend it not just with formidable conventional forces but with their own nuclear weapons . Ukraine has reminded us that in the long run there is no non-nuclear defence against a nuclear power . Through all this , Europe will change fundamentally and become a very different place . <p> What the Europeans can not credibly do is imagine that these changes can be avoided by waiting out Trump , hoping that in four years ' time everything will go back to the way they like to remember it . For one thing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and policy will ever return to " normal " . Even more fundamentally , whoever is in the White House , it simply defies the laws of political gravity that the US will ever again shoulder the burden of defending Europe -- including against the risks of nuclear war -- when its own security does not depend on it . <p> This , of course , carries a big lesson for Australia . Like the Europeans , we have all too easily been lulled by Washington 's policy elites into believing they will do whatever it takes to defend their leadership of the Asian strategic order from the ambitions of a regional great power . We , too , have ignored the fundamental reality that , despite what the US says , the costs and risk to America of containing China far exceed the imperatives to do so . In particular , there is no way we can expect the US to fight a nuclear war to defend its allies in Asia , and that means there is no way it can deter or defeat China 's challenge . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and maybe sooner -- we will find ourselves facing our gravest strategic reckoning in generations , as the Europeans do right now , wondering how we can defend ourselves without the US . @@122103449 <h> Sam Roggeveen Why Australia 's response to China must be measured <p> On February 14 , exactly one week before China 's naval flotilla began live-fire drills off the coast of Eden , New South Wales , Japan 's defence minister released information about his nation 's interactions with the Chinese navy . In the previous year , Minister Gen Nakatani revealed , Chinese naval vessels had passed through the waters surrounding Japan 's southern islands 68 times en route to the Pacific Ocean . The data on Japanese contacts with China 's air force shows a comparably high tempo : in 2023 , Japan scrambled its fighter aircraft on 479 occasions to shadow Chinese aircraft operating near Japanese airspace . <p> Given these numbers , Japanese military officials must have observed with wry amusement the overwrought reaction to the three Chinese warships sailing off Australia 's east coast and then circumnavigating the continent . <p> This is not to downplay what China has done . To send a destroyer -- one of China 's largest and most modern -- a frigate , a replenishment ship and possibly a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ biggest city to disrupt air traffic is a novel and concerning development . Australians are right to take it seriously . Japan may be used to this kind of thing by now , but its defence forces have not always been so busy because China 's military has not always been this big , this active and this ambitious . Like Japan , Australia should expect Chinese activity near its shores and airspace to become more frequent . <p> Still , there are sound military and political reasons for Australia not to make too much of this affair . <p> Shadow defence minister Andrew Hastie used the term " gunboat diplomacy " to describe China 's naval deployment , and he has a point . Beijing was trying to send an intimidating message with its warships . China 's military brass did n't choose the route for this deployment randomly . It did so to make a statement about its new military capabilities and to signal to Australia and the region that the Pacific Ocean is no longer an American lake . <p> Yet , as worrying as it was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Australian mainland , the deployment also illustrates the limits of gunboat diplomacy . Take the Renhai-class destroyer that led the flotilla , one of the largest and most capable such ships in the world . It is equipped with 112 missile-launch canisters , stacked on their end beneath the deck of the ship so that all one sees from the outside is a neat grid of square lids , each one hinged . When the lid is flipped open , the missile stored beneath emerges in a plume of smoke and rocket fire . <p> As for the kind of missiles , the Renhai-class destroyer is designed primarily to create a bubble around itself and its accompanying fleet that no enemy can penetrate . The missile load would therefore typically be biased towards weapons that can sink ships and shoot down incoming aircraft and missiles . But the Renhai class can also carry some weapons used to hit land targets from long range -- Chinese equivalents of the Tomahawk cruise missiles that Australian destroyers now field . <p> What must be resisted is the occasional Australian compulsion , in moments @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ present moment , to retaliate against provocations . In such an unbalanced relationship , the larger party will always enjoy what strategists call escalation dominance , which basically means China can always up the ante . <p> If the Renhai carried , say , 30 such missiles , each with a 500-kilogram warhead , it could destroy a handful of large buildings in Sydney . That sounds terrifying , but in military terms it 's not a huge return on the effort and expense of making the arduous journey from China . If Australia and China were at war , we would be unlikely to buckle under that kind of pressure . Once the ship 's missile battery was exhausted , it would need to make the long trek home to re-arm . All the while , our navy and air force would stand a fighting chance of sinking these ships , which would make the return on investment look even less appealing for Beijing . <p> It 's important to stress that , even though this is a wartime scenario -- and an extremely unlikely one at that -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Australia conduct their peacetime relations . Gunboat diplomacy only works if the side being threatened with violence has a realistic fear that this violence will be on a scale it can not endure . That fear alone will drive their policy without a shot needing to be fired . In the present case , Australia can reasonably conclude that China 's gunboat diplomacy has failed because this fleet simply is n't strong enough to strike that kind of fear into us . <p> Of course , the fleets will get bigger as China 's navy continues to modernise and grow . In turn , that should drive Australia towards developing more formidable defences against them , and also against a Chinese air force with ambitions to field bombers that can reach Australia . Our aim should be to build a defence force capable of credibly signalling that , while Australia can never stop China from conducting provocative manoeuvres off our coast , they must be conducted on Australian terms , because China will know that , in the event of a crisis , those ships would be sent to the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ version of the " Defence of Australia " doctrine developed in the 1980s . Back then , of course , Australia had no worries about the reliability of its great ally , the United States , and China had yet to emerge as a maritime power that would eventually challenge American dominance . American reliability has been in doubt for some years , but the edifice crumbled a week ago in that infamous press conference pitting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky against President Donald Trump and his deputy , J. ? D. Vance . <p> Today , the job of defending Australia is harder because we need to plan on doing it independently and against a great power . The task is nevertheless achievable , because the technology of modern warfare favours us and because we are so far from China . The only way for Beijing to project a lot of military force against Australia is with big ships and long-range aircraft . The Ukraine war demonstrates it is possible to blunt both . Ukraine is winning the naval war against Russia despite not having a navy . Instead , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and this has worked spectacularly well against the Russian fleet . The air war , meanwhile , is at a stalemate , with neither side willing to risk sending crewed aircraft through the air defences of the other . <p> This is not a call to abolish the Royal Australian Navy ; our circumstances are different from Ukraine 's . What is needed is a strong , defensively oriented Australian military that can blunt an attack against us by making it too dangerous to operate aircraft and ships in our air and maritime approaches . <p> This is not a formula for winning but for making it too costly for China to win . It 's a constrained and narrow goal that wo n't set military hearts racing , but it is an appropriate posture for a middle power facing a great power , alone . <p> What must be resisted is the occasional Australian compulsion , in moments of stress in the relationship with China such as the present moment , to retaliate against provocations . In such an unbalanced relationship , the larger party will always enjoy what @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ always up the ante . Sure , Australia could respond to the Chinese flotilla by sending a destroyer into the Taiwan Strait to conduct missile drills , but that would escalate the dispute . China could then escalate again . China will always have more resources and therefore more capacity to keep upping the ante . It enjoys escalation dominance . <p> For a middle power such as Australia , escalating means losing . Of course , you can also lose by giving in . The appropriate settling point is somewhere in-between , where we practise a kind of stoicism . Thanks to the strength , flexibility and openness of Australia 's economic model , exporters affected by China 's bans found new markets @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sanctions amounted to a rounding error for the national economy . When Labor won office in 2022 , Beijing saw an opportunity to walk back these measures and pursue a less belligerent policy . <p> Unfortunately , Australian defence policy has yet to incorporate the lessons of its successful economic policy . The AUKUS project to equip the Royal Australian Navy with eight nuclear-powered submarines cuts directly against the stoic mindset . @@122103456 <h> ANALYSIS : Government guidance on the use of NDAs , aimed at greater transparency in the interests of victim-survivors of sexual harassment , appears to have had little impact . By Regina Featherstone . <h> NDAs and what #MeToo has n't changed <p> The government 's efforts to ensure greater transparency around non-disclosure agreements are failing , judging by the conflicting reports between agencies on how many times NDAs have been used to settle cases of alleged sexual harassment . <p> NDAs entered public consciousness at the height of the #MeToo movement in 2017 when women such as Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein 's former executive assistant , Zelda Perkins , broke hers to let the world know of his pattern of sexual harassment and cover-up . NDAs are agreements comprising confidentiality and non-disparagement terms that prevent victim-survivors from speaking about their experience or saying negative things about their employer or specific individuals . They are commonly used in out-of-court settlements . <p> Australia 's response to the #MeToo movement 's revelations about NDAs has been slow . Five years ago , in the landmark Respect ? @ ? Work @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to investigate and improve how workplaces prevent and respond to sexual harassment . No data was available on the prevalence of NDAs in settlements , and while Jenkins found they can be a helpful resolution tool , she also noted that NDAs " have often served to intimidate and silence victims , while concealing the behaviour of harassers " . <p> Her subsequent report recommended guidance be issued on NDA use and so , in late 2022 , the government published a note encouraging lawyers to take a " trauma-informed " approach to resolving sexual harassment claims -- meaning they should prioritise the impact of the incident and legal process on a victim-survivor over commercial and other interests . <p> The guidance also recommended that NDAs be used on a case-by-case basis rather than as a default . If confidentiality is to be used at all , the guidance states , it should be limited in time and scope , allowing for victim-survivors to speak about their experiences wherever possible . <p> The guidelines are not enforceable ; they are simply suggestions of best practice for lawyers . There is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nature , NDAs are private agreements , so tracking progress on their use is difficult . <p> It 's for this reason that I undertook some research with a colleague at the University of Sydney , in order to determine whether the government guidance on NDA use had been effective . <p> The answer was a resounding " no " . In a survey of 145 employment lawyers across the country , we found 75 per cent had never resolved a matter of sexual harassment with NDA terms that allowed the victim-survivor to speak about what had happened to them . A quarter of respondents had n't read the NDA guidance . Half of the corporate lawyers , and a third of lawyers acting on behalf of the claimants , had never advised a client that NDAs were not mandatory . <p> In February 2022 , then Australian Public Service commissioner Peter Woolcott introduced directions on a consultation process for out-of-court sexual harassment settlements . The directions were to ensure that any APS agency seeking a settlement including a confidentiality or non-disclosure provision must first consult with -- or report @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Those who have experienced sexual harassment need to know that if they speak up they wo n't be drawn into bad-faith negotiations . <p> The directions were " to ensure that there is accountability and assurance across the APS " and provide an advisory role for the commissioner as a neutral party between government agencies and federal public servants . It was also intended to guarantee that any NDA use considered the wellbeing of the person alleging harassment . <p> A total of two sexual harassment matters proposing the use of confidentiality or non-disclosure terms were raised to the APS commissioner between mid 2022 and late 2024 , according to new data obtained via administrative release . <p> This figure contrasts with evidence given by officials from the Attorney-General 's Department , who told a Senate estimates hearing in November 2024 that settlement terms for six sexual harassment matters were actually approved over the same period . Requests for clarification from the department have not been fulfilled . <p> The APS Commission 's spokesperson responded to the discrepancy by saying , " The data reported by the Attorney-General @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ settlement terms were approved by the Attorney-General or their delegate . " They added that the commission " is not aware which of those matters has settled and for those that have settled , whether the settlement agreement included a confidentiality or non-disclosure provision . It is a matter for the relevant agencies to consult and report relevant matters to the Commission . " <p> In addition to consulting with the APS commissioner , federal government agencies are required to report matters that constitute " significant issues " -- as defined by the legal services directions -- to the Attorney-General 's Department for oversight . A spokesperson for the attorney-general confirmed that " most workplace sexual assault and sexual harassment claims are ' significant legal issues ' and therefore settlements require the Attorney-General 's approval " . <p> If this is the case , then the Attorney-General 's Department should have a record of all sexual harassment claims against the federal government and its use of NDAs in those agreements . The problem is that " significant issues " are a grey area as they are currently defined -- they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not an issue is reportable " is a matter for each agency to assess , based on the nature of the claim " , according to the attorney-general 's spokesperson . <p> In last year 's Senate estimates , the Attorney-General 's Department testified it could n't confirm that its sexual harassment and NDA data reflected 100 per cent of the claims against the government . The Attorney-General 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ exception to this stance is where confidentiality " is necessary to protect the Commonwealth 's interests " . When The Canberra Times reported on this " loophole " , Dreyfus responded that the article " misrepresented " the government 's position . The definition of the " Commonwealth 's interests " remains unclear . <p> The lack of transparency surrounding these arrangements ought to be of public concern , not least because they are settled with public funds . <p> One solution may be to have streamlined oversight , with mandatory reporting to one central agency . By Mike Seccombe . <h> Coalition leads ' obstructionist ' forces on climate <p> On Monday morning , Tropical Cyclone Alfred seemed to be running out of puff . <p> About 300 kilometres off the Sunshine Coast and moving further away to the south-east , it was downgraded to a category 1 storm and seemed to be on the verge of breaking up . Then something extraordinary happened . <p> It rapidly reintensified . Following that , it radically changed course and began heading generally west towards Brisbane . <p> Science tells us that for a cyclone to form , it requires sea temperatures above 26.5 degrees -- hence the descriptor " tropical " cyclone . Once established , it 's not unusual for cyclones to travel beyond the tropics . They just do n't form , or in this case re-form , outside the tropics . <p> Alfred did , though , and the reason @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , 500 kilometres south of the Tropic of Capricorn , was a balmy 27 degrees . <p> " Meteorologists and climate scientists are likely to study Alfred for years to come , " says Matt Kean , chair of the Climate Change Authority , the independent statutory body charged with advising government on climate policy . <p> " Yes , there have been rare cyclones that have passed through that corner of eastern Australia in the past , but the behaviour of a storm that should have broken up but re-formed off Brisbane ... it will be scrutinised carefully . " <p> Kean was speaking with The Saturday Paper on Wednesday and was careful not to sound insensitive to the human dimension of what was to unfold . The politics of the situation are undeniable , though , at this point in world affairs . <p> " We hope and pray residents in south-east Queensland and northern New South Wales are going to make it through this storm unscathed . @@122103470 <h> Brett Sheehy 's penultimate Adelaide Festival is an array of powerful performances , from its stunning opera centrepiece to a primeval flamenco . By Alison Croggon . <h> Treasures feature in the opening weekend of Adelaide Festival 2025 <p> No one can say that the Adelaide Festival artistic director , Brett Sheehy , is n't hands-on . As the obligatory pre-performance housekeeping announcement floated over Adelaide 's auditoriums , I thought , That voice sounds familiar . It turns out that it is Sheehy himself , an anonymous presence before every show . <p> Sheehy , who is among other things the former artistic director of Melbourne Theatre Company , represents a steadying interregnum in what has been a volatile time at the Adelaide Festival . He stepped into the breach after Ruth Mackenzie departed in 2024 , only a year into her tenure , to become a cultural policy wonk in the South Australian government . Mackenzie herself took over from Neil Armfield and Rachel Healy after their surprise 2022 departures . In 2026 , it was announced this week , the current Malthouse artistic director , Matthew @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ delivered a solid program of performance , studded with familiar names -- international luminaries such as Tanztheater Wuppertal Pina Bausch and Forced Entertainment , balanced with works by prominent Australian artists such as Lucy Guerin Inc , Stephanie Lake and bestselling author Trent Dalton . Not a lot this year is particularly out there , but there 's no denying that the opening weekend featured some treasures . <p> The big ticket , as always , is an opera : this time the most exciting offering for years . Innocence is Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho 's final work , written before her death at 70 in 2023 . It 's directed by Simon Stone , who began his substantial career in Melbourne 's rich independent theatre scene in the early 2000s where , with current Melbourne Theatre Company artistic director Anne-Louise Sarks and others , he founded one of the best indie companies of the time , The Hayloft Project . Since leaving Australia in the 2010s he has become a major director on the European and now American stages . He 's returned , very self-evidently at the height @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ masterpiece . <p> From the moment conductor Cl ? ment Mao-Takacs summons the first rumbling bass piano chord , presaging a score rich in the drama of woodwinds and percussion , you know you 're in for something special . Sofi Oksanen 's Finnish libretto is intertwined with a libretto by Aleksi Barri ? re in several languages -- English , German , Greek , French and Spanish . The whole functions like a lyric play , creating a kind of domestic psychological realism . In lesser hands this might have made for a dire experience , because it slows the action down to singing pace : but here the pacing works with the music as an emotional intensifier . <p> Across two fluid timelines , Innocence follows the harrowing story , before and after , of a school shooting . We open with a wedding : Stela ( Faustine de Mon ? s ) , an outsider , is marrying Tuomas ( Sean Panikkar ) . The wedding party is suspiciously small , and it becomes clear very soon that a dark secret is being kept from the bride @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is employed at the last minute when someone is taken ill . Gradually she reveals that her daughter , Mark ? ta ( Erika Hammarberg ) , was killed by the absent son of the family . Meanwhile , in other rooms and other times , others recount their ongoing traumatic responses to a shooting 10 years before that occurred at an international school they attended as students . This story is fictional but it 's clearly inspired by two Finnish school shootings in 2007 and 2008 , in which 18 students were killed . <p> Chloe Lamford 's design is a two-storey contemporary house set on a revolve : we peer like voyeurs through the picture windows as everything unravels . Sometimes the building is the school , sometimes it is the family house . The action begins in the present in both through lines but moves fluidly like memory into the past . <p> Perhaps what 's most impressive about Saariaho 's music is its sheer range . Innocence is a work notable for sonic detail . By Carolyn Barnes . <h> Image Economies and how technology transforms <p> Monash University Museum of Art launches into its 50th year with the exhibition Image Economies . Featuring works from the Monash University Collection and new commissions , it showcases several generations of artists who have explored the role of images in shaping identities , subjectivities and social norms . <p> Curators Stephanie Berlangieri , Melanie Oliver and Francis E. Parker fulfil the assignment of a university art museum by challenging their audience with complex , multifaceted ideas . Many works employ video and digital installations that require extended engagement from the viewer . <p> Image Economies emphasises the deep connection between representation and technology , and how technology amplifies and transforms our experience of images . For example , Ian Burn 's Systematically Altered Photographs ( 1968 ) , the exhibition 's earliest work , is basic compared with other works . Yet photocopying transformed how we reproduce and share ideas , while its convenience @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ assumptions about photographic truth , Burn repeatedly photocopied images from a government brochure celebrating Australia 's development until only traces of the originals remained . The work is complemented by a theoretical text on the linguistic construction of visual experience . Here Burn deploys the photocopy to prioritise concept and process over the idealisation of the original artwork . <p> Conceptual artists such as Burn addressed fundamental issues within representation through cool philosophical analysis . Artists active from the late 1970s extended this to scrutinise whole systems of representation across the high/low cultural divide . Jeff Gibson 's series disPOSTERS ( 1986 ) exemplifies how artists appropriated and recontextualised mass cultural imagery to question the control of the production of meaning in industries such as advertising , media and entertainment . The paired images in Gibson 's work are visual tropes , formulaic elements found in multiple contexts to convey normative ideas and attitudes , which question the pervasive influence of mass media on society . <p> The most arresting works are by artists who use digital media to explore issues obliquely through emotions , sensations and mood . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at traditional depictions of women . Yet Todorov 's subjects have some agency in crafting their public image , simultaneously challenging and reinforcing societal expectations . In Heaven ( 1997 ) , Tracey Moffatt films male surfers changing out of their wetsuits in beach-side car parks . By positioning the audience to view the surfers through a voyeuristic lens , Moffatt flips the male gaze , making the surfers the subjects of visual pleasure . <p> The most arresting works are by artists who use digital media to explore issues obliquely through emotions , sensations and mood . @@122103476 <h> Hoosiers and the brilliance of Gene Hackman <p> My fondness for Hoosiers is largely a mystery to me , given how doggedly formulaic it is . Few of its characters are written as humans , rather as types , and the same goes for the tiny Midwestern town where it 's set -- idyllic in ways but made up of suspicious locals whose detachment from the rest of the country is a source of both pride and insecurity . <p> Yet I agree with the conventional wisdom that it 's one of the best sports films ever made . One unmysterious reason for that is the performance of the late Gene Hackman . <p> It 's 1951 and a talented coach , used to bigger cities and higher stakes , moves to the fictional Hickory , Indiana , a town of barely 1000 people that rarely features on state maps . Coach Norman Dale has torched his reputation , and seemingly his career , with some ( initially ) unnamed scandal , and has spent the previous decade in the navy . His appointment as Hickory High School 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ opportunity -- though one he 'll have to seize with a modest squad and against an immodestly hostile town . <p> That hostility assumes different forms . The most sophisticated is expressed by a fellow teacher , Myra Fleener ( Barbara Hershey ) , who tells Dale there are only two reasons a man moves to Hickory : because he 's escaping something or because he 's got nowhere else to go . <p> She 's not wrong , and her animus is deepened by her assumption that Dale will attempt to recruit the town 's best player , Jimmy Chitwood . A fatherless boy , Jimmy has left the team while grieving over the death of its former coach , who served as a surrogate dad . Fleener is protective of the boy , whose talents extend beyond basketball , and she 's defensively pre-empting his exploitation . <p> The hostility of the other townsfolk is less sophisticated . They 've got used to a certain arrangement : they have access to training sessions , their various cockamamie thoughts on tactics are indulged by the coach , and their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a specific way . <p> Coach Dale is wilful and yields nothing to these gripes , which only makes the townsfolk angrier . Myra Fleener , though , is a person who can be persuaded by the evidence of her own eyes , and she comes to revise her initial assessment and see Dale as a man of unusual integrity . <p> You could probably have guessed all this . An outsider comes to a small town in search of redemption and is thwarted by a modest inheritance and the parochial suspicions of locals . Success will require an implacable faith in his own talents -- and the support of the less obnoxiously reactionary locals when they discern his decency . <p> There 's also the town drunk , Shooter , a former high-school prospect who knows more than anyone else about basketball . His distinction in the town is a sad one and he lives alone in a decrepit shack with his dogs and whisky . He can be seen at local games , though , where he 'll often disgrace himself with drunken meltdowns -- mortally embarrassing his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by the electric Dennis Hopper , Shooter 's too far gone to even desire redemption -- instead , it 's something Coach Dale offers him when he recognises Shooter 's strategic wisdom in the moments when his intelligence is not blighted by liquor . <p> Hoosiers , which was released in 1986 , was inspired by one of Indiana 's most famous basketball stories -- the so-called " Miracle of Milan " of 1954 when the state high-school championship was won by the smallest-ever school to have done so . <p> The consolidation of high schools had barely begun by then in Indiana , meaning there were almost 800 schools of wildly varying size . Milan High School ( pronounced " My-lin " ) had just 161 students at the time ; the four-time champions they played in the final , Muncie Central , had almost 2000 . <p> Australians might not appreciate the ardency of support for sub-professional leagues in the United States , not only for college competitions but also high-school ones . In 1954 , in a state famous for its obsession with basketball , the high-school @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Milan won 32-30 with a last-second jump shot by Bobby Plump , a scene re-created in Hoosiers . Not re-created , however , was Plump 's earlier holding of the ball for a good four minutes to run the clock down and confer a breather to his teammates , who were less athletic than their opponents . Such a dismal tactic was possible before the days of the shot clock . <p> Milan High School 's coach then was Marvin Wood who , at 24 , was much younger than Hackman 's Dale . Much less volatile , too , and not in need of a redemptive last chance . He left Milan High School with a record of 52-7 , and left the world in 1999 , aged 71 . " You knew he meant business , " Plump said at the time of Wood 's death . " He coached with quiet confidence and dignity . " <p> Hoosiers opens with Coach Dale driving alone through the large Midwestern cornfields to Hickory in a gorgeously unhurried sequence . The mythic openness is captured and so too @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ men shooting at crude hoops affixed to barns . <p> All of this will sound familiar : it 's the sentimental iconography of the Midwest , in which artful cinematography hopes to suggest through image alone a sense of the region 's mysterious nobility and plainness of spirit . In this simple idyll , not one smokestack or polluted sunset will be seen . Here , things are green , lush and fertile . <p> The sentimentality of the film 's images , and its story , are neatly contrasted with the bitterness of its locals . It is largely instinctive and dumb -- a measure of parochial defensiveness . This , of course , is a cinematic type itself -- and never given any grounding or explanation by the film 's writer -- but the sour prejudice of locals at least offers an interesting contrast with the beauty of their environment . <p> Hoosiers also clips along -- there 's an impressive momentum to the film . It 's especially impressive given that it was the directorial debut of David Anspaugh , and the first script by its writer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by its delighted attention to period detail . The uniforms and gyms , for instance , or when one can glimpse , very briefly , the wry , hand-drawn sign above the head of the team 's bus driver : " In the event of Rapture , this bus will be without a driver . " <p> I suspect , though , that the film 's success owes largely to Gene Hackman , whose partially mummified body was found alongside that of his wife , Betsy Arakawa , on February 26 ( US time ) in their Santa Fe home in strange -- and for now unresolved -- circumstances . <p> I wo n't speculate on those circumstances here . Enough to say that Hackman was a legend who invested most of his roles with unusual gravity -- even those he 'd later say he took on for the money alone . <p> I confess that the mechanics of the actor 's craft is largely mysterious to me . @@122125335 <p> Scientists can interact naturally , providing ideas or feedback to guide AI research <p> Artificial intelligence has already had a major impact on scientific research by accelerating discoveries , improving accuracy , and handling vast datasets that would be near-impossible for humans to analyze efficiently . AI-powered algorithms can assist in the discovery of new drugs , optimize materials for energy storage , and aid in modeling climate change . <p> A number of projects have been set up to make AI more useful and more reliable in a scientific setting . We 've previously written about the concept of the " exocortex , " which aims to provide a bridge between the human mind and a network of AI agents , and more recently , an Australian research team developed a generative AI tool called LLM4SD ( Large Language Model for Scientific Discovery ) , designed to speed up scientific breakthroughs . <p> Now , Google is also launching a similar initiative , which aims to turn AI into a co-scientist that can accelerate scientific discoveries . The tech giant explains , " The AI co-scientist is a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collaborative tool for scientists . " <h> Deploying specialized scientific agents <p> The AI co-scientist is built on Google 's Gemini 2.0 and is the result of collaboration between Google Research , Google DeepMind , and Google Cloud AI teams . It is designed to " mirror the reasoning process underpinning the scientific method . " Google says that its system is intended to " uncover new , original knowledge and to formulate demonstrably novel research hypotheses and proposals , building upon prior evidence and tailored to specific research objectives . " <p> The system will use a number of specialized agents - Generation , Reflection , Ranking , Evolution , Proximity , and Meta-review - that can iteratively generate , evaluate , and refine hypotheses . Google says that scientists will be able to interact with the system in whatever way best suits their needs . This will include providing their own seed ideas or feedback on generated outputs in natural language . <p> Not wishing to rush its deployment , the company plans to offer access to the system for research organizations through a trusted tester program . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news , opinion , features and guidance your business needs to succeed ! <p> Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsBy submitting your information you agree to the Terms &amp; Conditions and Privacy Policy and are aged 16 or over . <p> Wayne Williams is a freelancer writing news for TechRadar Pro . @@122196793 <p> The Australian Government has added 21 new species of fauna and flora to the threatened species list , with six more being uplisted to higher threat categories . This decision underscores Australia 's worsening extinction crisis as the nation continues to grapple with one of the worst extinction rates in the world . <p> " This announcement shows that species like the Irwin 's turtle , named after famed conservationist Steve Irwin , are now threatened with extinction due to the impacts of disease , habitat destruction and the impacts of invasive species , " says James Trezise , the Director of the Biodiversity Council . <p> " A number of species listed , such as the western mud minnow , are increasingly being impacted by drought and temperature extremes , highlighting the threats that our native wildlife face due to climate change , " says Trezise . <p> Under the EPBC Act , any species added to the threatened list becomes a ' national matter of environmental significance . ' In theory , this means that any project or development with the potential to impact these species must @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ formulates conservation advice and recommends recovery and threat abatement plans . <p> " Unfortunately , in this country , listing species as at risk of extinction does not currently guarantee protection from harm or resources ( funding ) to support recovery , " says Director of the Melbourne Biodiversity Institute and Biodiversity Council Lead Councillor Brendan Wintle . <p> " Habitats of endangered species continue to be destroyed , and funding to protect and support the recovery of threatened species is pitifully inadequate . @@122197073 <p> It is deeply weird that one of Labor 's most expansive climate policies is also one of its least mentioned . The " safeguard mechanism " -- a policy that purportedly limits the greenhouse gas emitted by Australia 's heavy industry and fossil mining facilities -- covers a full third of Australia 's domestic emissions . Yet it barely exists in public discourse . Why ? <p> Safeguard has a grim origin , with Labor having rejigged a Coalition policy instead of designing its own ( wedging opponents takes precedence over deploying policy that works ) . Safeguard 's progenitor , the Coalition 's " emissions reduction fund " , set limits high above actual emissions ( amusingly , as emissions rose , these limits often gently floated upwards ) . <p> It was an IKEA houseplant : it looked real , but only from a great distance . <p> Due to the higher climate policy standards faced by Labor , it had to achieve the same goal using different tactics . The carbon offsetting industry came to the rescue . <p> Like the old scheme , safeguard sets @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , these targets fall over time , meaning theoretically the facility should cut its pollution to comply . Naturally , there 's a glaring loophole : a company can meet the targets even when its pollution is above the limit by purchasing an equivalent number of Australian carbon offsets . <p> Another option is that overperforming facilities which are under their target can " trade " credit units with others over theirs , but this is unlikely in the short term ( and would be more expensive for a polluter than just buying normal offsets ) . <p> Safeguard is frequently defended ( and derided ) as a form of " carbon pricing " -- being forced to pay for offsets is a financial disincentive against high emissions . Offsets are exceedingly cheap , have the added benefit of fake neutralisation of your climate damage , and fossil fuel companies swimming in record-breaking super profits only use a tiny fraction of those profits for the required number of offsets . Worst of all , the money ends up in the pockets of carbon trading corporations , rather than the government @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pushed for real emissions cuts , but Labor won the vibes contest . Tuning safeguard to mandate real , deep emissions cuts was decried as excessive perfectionism that would resurface Australia 's mythical " climate wars " . <p> Once safeguard passed , it was memory-holed . It only gets exhumed when Labor tries to defend its passivity around the expansion of coal and gas . When Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was pushed on including a " climate trigger " in mine approvals , he muttered that " climate issues are dealt with through the safeguard mechanism " . When Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek was pressed on the same , she dismissed it , saying , " The safeguard mechanism is the way that we deal with carbon emissions in this country ... it 's bringing down carbon emissions . " <p> Safeguard came into effect July 1 , 2023 , and we wo n't get official data on its first full financial year of operations until April 15 . However , we can prod existing data to check if it really is " bringing down carbon emissions " . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Looking at the sectors that cover heavy industry in Australia ( with the caveat that non-safeguard facilities are covered here too ) , there has been zero noticeable difference to each sector 's greenhouse gas emissions from mid-2023 through to the end of 2024 : <p> ( Credit : Ketan Joshi ) <p> A Climate Change Authority ( CCA ) " progress report " examined the first year of safeguard in detail using preliminary data , and found 153 of the covered 215 facilities had emissions higher than the limit set by the Clean Energy Regulator . Thirty-one of those facilities exceeded their limits by 30% . In aggregate , all of the sites that are meant to be regulated by this scheme emitted 10.7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent above the total limit . <p> In short : no change beyond business as usual , despite the new targets . But the massive , widespread beaching of targets means the guaranteed mass purchase of " Australian carbon credit units " , or ACCUs . <p> Safeguard is an incredible demand fabrication engine for carbon offsets . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ compliance with the scheme will be met using offsets instead of real emissions reductions out to 2030 . " Safeguard facilities ' reliance on ACCUs to meet obligations is forecast to drive ACCU demand out to 2030 . ACCU prices are forecast to increase as a result of the growth in demand for ACCUs " , the report says . <p> The CCA offers a confident forecast of future carbon offset profits , and a nervous shrug about whether real emissions will be cut . That is before it details that there will be 31 million tonnes of new emissions to be added to the scheme 's coverage up to 2030 , 21 million of which relate to coal , oil and gas " carbon bomb " projects . <p> While it 's almost certain the first year of the scheme did nothing for real emissions , it has already created a massive surge in demand for Australia 's highly criticised carbon offsetting scheme . The Clean Energy Regulator 's new quarterly report reveals the growing stockpiles of carbon offsets specifically for meeting the safeguard mechanism 's ratcheting targets : @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ emitters in safeguard can pay a pittance to indefinitely comply with the scheme . But they still consider it an irritation and have restarted calls for compliance to be opened up to allow cheap international carbon offsets -- even more controversial than Australia 's heavily criticised scheme . <p> Profits for carbon markets thrive in two conditions : " ambitious " net-zero targets paired with zero will to actually reduce emissions . Voluntary targets are already starting to shudder and shift thanks to the unashamed fossil-fascist permission space of TrumpWorld 2025 . If Peter Dutton were to become prime minister , he could wreck this regulatory capture paradise for Australia 's fossil fuel and offsetting industries . Equally , Dutton might recognise the value of mandated greenwashing schemes . The offsets lobby is already pleading with him to keep it in place . <p> You are n't meant to look too closely at the safeguard mechanism . The formulas , acronyms and faux-complexity are there to obscure the simple dual stories of protectionism and cronyism from two massive , interlocking fossil/offsetting industries . <p> It 's a plastic houseplant : @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vaguely like something real and respiring . <p> Have something to say about this article ? @@122212911 <h> EV owners used their batteries on wheels to power homes amid Alfred blackouts <p> In the midst of Cyclone Alfred and its aftermath , there were upwards of 450,000 homes in south-east Queensland and north east NSW blacked out at some point over the past week . Even a few days after Alfred became an ex-tropical cyclone , there were still more than 120,000 properties without power . <p> But some houses -- including those with home batteries and EV owners with vehicle to load technology -- were able to keep their appliances going and their lights on . And the EV owners in particular have been taking to social media to report how their batteries on wheels helped them power their homes through the storm . <p> Vehicle-to-load ( V2L ) technology allows power to be sent from a car 's battery to external appliances -- though not all EVs have V2L capability , including Australia 's two most popular EVs to date , the Tesla Model Y and the Model 3 . <p> Chris Baker , director of Sunshine Hydro , a company proposing to combine pumped @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Queensland , took to LinkedIn to share that his 2013 Nissan leaf had kept the lights and fridges running . <p> " With a simple inverter connected to the 12V battery , we 're keeping food fresh , phones charged , and laptops going , " Baker wrote . " The Leaf stays switched on so it continues to recharge the 12V system from the main battery . <p> " This moment is a reminder of how energy is n't just about supply , but about orchestration -- bringing together all available resources to keep things running when they matter most . <p> " It 's also a lesson that energy storage , not just energy production , is the backbone of energy resilience . " <p> Meanwhile , in a post in Hyundai EV Enthusiasts Australia , one EV owner said his family had been , " saved by our 24 Kona EV " . <p> The Brisbane-based family , who were flooded in without power for two and a half days , connected an extension cord into the car and were able to power their fridge and freezer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ them get by while also providing cups of coffee for their neighbours . <p> That poster said they had currently used about 18 per cent of their battery power , and he estimated they 'd have been able to keep afloat for another few days had the power not been switched back on . <p> Meanwhile , another poster in an MG4 owners ' group on Facebook said his family had relied on their MG4 for power for 36 hours , over which time they 'd been able to run " a beast of a fridge , devices , kettle , and my coffee machine ( vital ) " . <p> That poster said that with his household 's consumption they 'd lost about 10 per cent of their capacity per day , and would probably have been able to last a week if needed . <p> Another poster on a remote property talked of using his EV to power the house , and being able to drive down to an area where grid power was available , topping up the EV battery , and then driving home to power @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ relying on your EV for power would be a future devoid of power outages -- but in the face of natural disasters , which in Australia can range from floods to fires to heatwaves , and which are predicted to increase , the electric vehicle may take over the role of power saviour from the trusty old generator . <p> Professor Jake Whitehead , head of policy at the Electric Vehicle Council , is based in Brisbane . On Saturday , having lost power to his home , Whitehead 's household were able to use both their Kia EV9 and Ford F-150 Lightning to run appliances . <p> " Clearly , Australia is quite exposed in terms of the impact of natural disasters , and with climate change we expect that both the frequency and severity of those types of events is only going to increase , " Whitehead said . " So , we need to be resilient to it . @@122239721 <p> Despite all this , the damage could have been so much worse -- and we may not be so lucky next time . Australia must use Cyclone Alfred as a serious wake-up call to bolster our essential infrastructure against disasters . <h> Cyclone : A complex picture <p> Cyclones are incredibly complex . They involve multiple interacting hazards such as severe wind , flooding , storm surge and erosion . This makes their impacts hard to predict . <p> Alfred meandered slowly off the coast for almost a fortnight , fed by warm waters in the Coral Sea . Its movements were made even more complicated by a new moon , which creates extra-high high tides . <p> Despite these intricacies , experts were able to map the path and character of the cyclone . This was due to collaboration between multiple agencies and personnel across national , state and local governments . <h> Drawing lessons from nature <p> As climate change worsens , extreme weather will become more frequent and severe . We must minimise the risks of infrastructure failing during these events . It will require a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ past . <p> Nature is incredibly resilient . It can offer many lessons to decision-makers , engineers , town planners and others . This approach is known as " biomimicry " -- innovation that emulates the forms , processes or systems found in nature . <p> Connected vegetation such as a line of mature trees , wetlands and mangroves can detain and slow water . This means water passing through has less energy to erode land and topple infrastructure . It also allows for water to soak into the ground , which cleans it and filters out debris . <p> In flood management , holding ponds known as " detention basins " are used to temporarily store stormwater run-off during heavy rain . City parks can be reshaped or upgraded to become detention basins , holding water until it can safely drain away . <p> Urban infrastructure could also mimic the swales and earthen mounds found in nature , by incorporating human-made channels and mounds . These would guide water away from communities and infrastructure , to storage above or underground . <p> And what about our coastlines ? Cyclones @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ out beaches . Alfred has left extreme sand erosion up and down the coast . <p> Coastlines are inherently mobile ; sand naturally leaves and returns , depending on the weather . To protect our permanent coastal development , sand dune restoration could provide a line of defence in front of built infrastructure . This option has been implemented in the Netherlands , where it was found to be cost-effective . <p> In Australia , an estimated 17% of mangroves have been destroyed since European settlement . Mangroves naturally buffer the land from wind and storm surge . Reinstating mangroves could help protect coastal communities from future wind damage , as a 2020 study in Fiji showed . <p> Globally , there is a growing movement towards creating " sponge cities " . These are urban areas rich in natural features such as trees , lakes and parks , which can absorb rain ( and sometimes wind ) and prevent flooding . <p> Australia is cottoning on to how nature can help protect our cities . But there is much more work to do . <p> Experts from James Cook @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ data after ex-Cyclone Alfred . They are documenting the effects of extreme wind and other hazards on buildings and infrastructure , and collecting data on wind speeds , water ingress and damage caused by debris . <p> Hopefully , the findings will inform decision-making on construction , building codes and disaster-resilience strategies for communities . <h> Building back better <p> Climate change is expected to cause fewer , but generally more severe , tropical cyclones . Combined with other climate-related changes , such as more intense rainfall and higher sea levels , the risk of flooding associated with cyclones will worsen .
