@@122255879 <h> Heat Pump vs . Furnace : Which Is Best for Your Home ? <p> These two heating systems have their strengths and weaknesses -- pick the best for your special circumstances . <p> Erin GoblerContributor <p> Erin Gobler is a personal finance writer based in Madison , Wisconsin . She writes about topics including budgeting , student loans , credit , mortgages , investing and insurance . Her work has been published in financial publications and startups such as NextAdvisor , The Simple Dollar , LendingTree , Robinhood and more . <p> Mike De Socio is a CNET contributor who writes about energy , personal finance and climate change . He 's also the author of the nonfiction book , " Morally Straight : How the Fight for LGBTQ+ Inclusion Changed the Boy Scouts-And America . " His path in journalism has taken him through almost every part of the newsroom , earning awards along the way from the Boston Press Photographers Association and the Society of Professional Journalists . As an independent journalist , his work has also been published in Bloomberg , The Guardian , Fortune and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ awards from the Boston Press Photographers Association , the Society of Professional Journalists and Boston University <p> When you think about why you need to control the temperature of your home , the heat keeping your home items from freezing in the winter is probably a key reason you think of . To get heat in the home , there are a few options to choose from , heat pump or furnace . The best option for your situation will vary based on which advantages are most beneficial to your home and area . <p> Here , we 'll explore the primary differences between a heat pump and a furnace , including their cost , installation , performance and more . Then , we 'll help you decide which is right for you . <h> What is a heat pump ? <p> A heat pump is an energy-efficient alternative to a furnace and air conditioner . A heat pump uses electricity to transfer heat from a cool space to a warm one . In the winter , it takes the heat from outdoors and uses it to heat your home @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inside your home to outside to cool your home . <p> " The best way to describe a heat pump is an air conditioner with a reversing valve , " said Melanie Powers , president at Goodberlet Home Services . <p> A heat pump is more efficient than a furnace because it does n't actually generate heat -- it simply relocates it . Although it does n't generate heat , it can still provide a comfortable temperature in your home . <p> There are several different types of heat pumps that you should know about : <p> An air-source heat pump is the most common type . It sucks air through a coil which helps either heat or cool your home by transferring air between the inside and outside . <p> A ground-source heat pump , also known as geothermal , operates along the same lines -- transferring heat from outside to inside , or vice versa -- but draws its heat from underground wells , rather than from the air . <p> A gas-source heat pump , which is less popular , is similar to an air-source heat pump @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ production in the unit , according to Powers . <h> What is a furnace ? <p> A furnace is the type of heating system that most homeowners are more familiar with . This home appliance uses fuel -- often natural gas , which consists primarily of the fossil fuel methane -- to generate heat in your home . Using either a pilot light or an electronic ignition , your furnace creates hot air and blows it through your home . <p> The primary components of a furnace are the burner that burns the fuel , the heat exchangers that transfer the heat , a blower fan to distribute the heat in your home , and a flue to serve as an exhaust for gaseous by-products . <p> Here , too , there are different types of furnaces depending on the type of fuel they use . <p> A gas furnace is the most common type . " It 's a much warmer heat than an electric furnace , " Powers said , because burning gas creates higher temperatures than electricity alone . One downside is that these furnaces generate carbon @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ must be vented properly to keep your home safe . <p> A propane furnace is more or less the same as a natural gas furnace but burns propane instead . These furnaces can be more efficient than natural gas , but those gains might not matter when propane is the more expensive fuel . And again , carbon monoxide is a concern here . <p> An electric furnace uses electricity to warm up a heat bank that boosts the temperature of the air before blowing it through your home . The advantage here is that there 's no combustion , and therefore no risk of fire or carbon monoxide poisoning in your home . <p> The most advantageous type of fuel for a furnace also depends on current energy prices . When electricity rates are high , a gas or propane furnace might win out . But the opposite is true if gas or propane prices surge . <h> Heat pump vs. furnace <h> Cost <p> One of the first questions that homeowners are likely to ask when comparing a heat pump and a furnace is which costs more . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is already equipped for . Homes with direct access to gas may find that a furnace is more affordable . On the other hand , a home without gas access will likely pay more to install the furnace . Everything else being equal , a heat pump is usually more affordable . <h> Maintenance <p> While both a heat pump and a furnace will require some recurring maintenance , the maintenance requirements for a furnace are lower than those for a heat pump . As a result , your long-term maintenance costs will also be greater for your heat pump . <p> The colder it gets , the more difficult it is for the heat pump to transfer heat . " Heat pumps just really are n't good in certain climates , " Powers said . Meanwhile , a furnace will continue to generate heat even in cold climates . <h> Energy usage <p> One of the greatest benefits of a heat pump is its energy efficiency . As we 've mentioned , furnaces generate heat while heat pumps only transfer it . As a result , heat pumps need @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ remember that heat pumps have to work harder than furnaces in cold weather to keep your home warm . If you live in a cold climate , a furnace may actually be more energy efficient . <h> Expected lifespan <p> A properly maintained gas furnace can have a lifespan of 20 years or more . On the other hand , even a well-maintained heat pump heater will have a lifespan closer to 15 years . <h> Appearance <p> If you already have a central air conditioning system in your home , swapping it for a heat pump ( which , remember , also provides A/C ) would n't change the appearance of your home at all . <p> " You would not know the difference between an air conditioner and a heat pump , they look exactly the same , " Powers said , referring to the boxy unit that would sit outside your home . <p> If your home does n't already have ductwork from an A/C , you might end up installing a mini-split heat pump system , which does have more of an aesthetic impact . With @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to install , but the other half of the system consists of wall-mounted units throughout your house that blow air into each zone . <p> With furnaces , the actual heating unit usually lives out of sight in your basement or attic . Two pipes need to run out the side of your house for proper ventilation , Powers said , which does impact the appearance of your house . <h> Installation <p> If you 're retrofitting an existing home , installation depends on what you already have . <p> Again , if you already have ductwork from an A/C system , installing a heat pump is an easy swap , and it 's unlikely to be invasive or costly . If your home does n't have ductwork , you 'd be more likely to get mini-split heat pumps , which avoid the cost and inconvenience of installing ductwork . <p> Furnaces also require ductwork , and installing it from scratch would involve ripping up walls to install the ducts and vents . <h> Tax incentives <p> The federal government is currently helping homeowners cover a significant chunk of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Inflation Reduction Act cover up to 30% of the cost of heat pumps and high-efficiency furnaces . You can ask your installer if the system you want qualifies for the credit , which could significantly change the cost calculus . <p> There might also be incentives offered on the state level , or by your local utility company , Powers said . Sometimes those incentives cover the heating system itself , but there are also smaller rebates for parts like a variable-speed blower motor for furnaces , Powers said . <p> Watch this : Be smart and save money warming your home this winter <p> 01:04 <h> The bottom line : Which is better for you ? <p> For more moderate climates , heat pumps are the clear winner . In " southern states , heat pumps are fantastic ... The more heat you have outside , the better these are operating , " said Powers . That 's because , as long as temperatures usually do n't dip below freezing , heat pumps are really efficient at transferring heat into your home . <p> In northern climates , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a furnace , or a special inverter heat pump that can perform in lower temperatures but is also more expensive . Powers said it really comes down to this question : " Do I have the right climate for this to be energy efficient ? " <p> Your decision could also be swayed by local financial incentives . All else being equal , an extra $1,000 off a heat pump could make that the obvious choice .

That meant customers had to be willing to front the full price of an EV and get a rebate months later . <p> But thanks to a rule change in 2024 , participating car dealers can now apply the discount at the point of sale , meaning the customer sees a reduction in the sticker price and there 's no need for you to file paperwork later . <h> These EVs qualify for the federal tax credit right now <p> The qualifying rules became more strict in 2025 , which is why the list of eligible EVs got smaller . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ meet to qualify for the credit . Some of them are typical income and price limits , but others relate to where EV batteries are manufactured and where the materials come from . <p> Here is the most current list of qualifying EVs for purchases made after Jan.1 , 2025 , and before Jan. 1 , 2026. <h> 2025 EV tax credit requirements <p> The idea behind these requirements is twofold : To make sure the credits are going to people who need them and to incentivize domestic manufacturing of electric vehicles . <h> MSRP <p> The tax credit has two caps on manufacturer 's suggested retail price , essentially the sticker price of the car . The limit is $80,000 for vans , sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks , and $55,000 for all other EVs . To claim the tax credit , the total price of the vehicle has to be less than those thresholds . <h> Critical minerals and battery component <p> Here 's where the requirements get tricky . To qualify for the credit , at least 60% of the " critical minerals " in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the US or a country that has a free trade agreement with the US . And at least 60% of the EV 's battery components must have been manufactured or assembled in the US or a country with a free trade agreement with the US . <h> Income limits <p> The credit is available only to those who make less than a certain amount in " adjusted gross income . " For married couples , the limit is $300,000 per year . For heads of households , the cap is $225,000 . And for all others , the limit is $150,000 in annual income . <h> Assembly location <p> Any EVs that are eligible for the federal discount must " undergo final assembly " in North America ( the US , Mexico or Canada ) . <h> How will Trump 's policies affect the EV tax credit ? <p> Despite the impression given by Trump 's many executive orders , the EV tax credit is part of the Inflation Reduction Act , which was created through an act of Congress and would require an act of Congress to repeal . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to get Congress to eliminate the EV tax credit , but for now it is still in place . <p> While Trump has been antagonistic toward EVs , it 's worth noting who benefits from the EV tax credit . For one : Trump ally Elon Musk 's Tesla , which has the most models of any brand eligible for the discount . " Telsa wins more than any other automaker , " Glenn said . <h> How to claim the EV tax credit in 2024 <p> Because dealerships are now able to offer the tax credit as a discount off the sticker price , there are n't many steps for the customer after a vehicle purchase . <p> Here 's what to know before you buy if you want to use the 2025 EV tax credit . <p> Not all dealerships offer the instant tax credit upfront . " There are some conditions there . A dealer can give you this , but the customer actually needs to understand " their income , Glenn said . Otherwise , the IRS could claw back the tax credit if you 're above the income limit . <p> Do n't forget about state-level EV rebates , which could be stacked on top of the federal credit . @@122295885 <h> Bong Joon-ho 's Mickey 17 dies a thousand deaths <p> " Dyin ' ai n't much of a livin ' , boy , " Clint Eastwood once hissed in The Outlaw Josey Wales . He might have been referring to the hapless grunt at the centre of Bong Joon-ho 's new sci-fi film , Mickey 17 , which -- as comically gruesome analogies for the working grind go -- has a premise that 's hard to beat . <p> At the end of each life , Mickey 's corpse is unceremoniously dumped into a waste furnace with the rest of the trash and he 's simply reissued in a new version , flopping out of a high-tech human 3D printer like a hot dog onto the meat-factory floor . Even dying , it turns out , is no escape from labour . " Have a nice death , " a colleague cheerily farewells him at one point . " See you tomorrow . " <p> With his ambitious tale of loopy clones , intergalactic bugs and cartoon megalomaniacs , no one could accuse Bong of courting respectability in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ thriller that swept awards season and won the Academy Award for Best Picture . <p> The shapeshifting South Korean auteur has long been drawn to sci-fi concepts that traffic in the grotesque to take aim at capitalism , from his breakout creature feature The Host ( 2006 ) to his rollicking super-pig saga Okja ( 2017 ) , films that sacrificed nothing in the way of crowd-pleasing entertainment to make their satirical points . His biggest canvas yet , Mickey 17 returns to his eclectic genre leanings , even if something of that special Bong touch has been lost along the way . <p> Adapted from an acclaimed 2022 novel by American writer Edward Ashton , Mickey 17 is set in the not-too-distant tomorrow of 2054 , where failed politician turned cult leader Kenneth Marshall ( Mark Ruffalo ) -- part tele-evangelist , part dictator , all knucklehead -- has set out to establish a new-race colony on the remote ice planet of Niflheim . Having escaped mob bosses on Earth after he and his buddy 's macaroon start-up went under ( it 's a long story ) , Mickey @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of his job requirements , and is now on his 17th clone incarnation in almost five years . <p> Stuck at the bottom of an icy crevasse after a dangerous mission , Mickey is -- per standard operating procedure -- left to die . This time , he 's saved by a clan of indigenous creatures who the colonists dub " creepers " -- furry , hard-shelled insectoids who roam the snow and bear a striking , surely deliberate , resemblance to the Ohm of Hayao Miyazaki 's Nausica ? of the Valley of the Wind ( 1984 ) . <p> Assuming Mickey 17 has died his regular death , his bosses , eager to move ahead , print out Mickey No. 18 ( also Pattinson ) , who by some quirk of the reproduction process turns out to be a more aggressive version of the source material . Suddenly there are two of them , with very different personalities . That 's great news for Mickey 17 's security agent girlfriend , Nasha ( Naomi Ackie ) , who understandably jumps at the chance to have two hunks in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fight , " she instructs them -- though not so much for the clones . Since multiples have been outlawed , one of them has to die , and the alpha 18 is determined to make sure his dweeby predecessor does n't stick around . <p> In movies such as David Cronenberg 's Cosmopolis ( 2012 ) , the Safdie brothers ' Good Time ( 2017 ) and Claire Denis ' High Life ( 2018 ) -- and , let 's be honest , Catherine Hardwicke 's Twilight ( 2007 ) , because what could be more bizarre than playing a teen-idol vampire ? -- Pattinson has proved to be one of our weirdest , or at the very least goofiest , movie stars . Indulging in a spell of antagonistic , odd-couple comedy here , he has great chemistry with himself , as perhaps the only other performer willing to match his freak . <p> One ca n't help but admire the audacity of an Oscar-winning director running off with a reported $120 million in studio money and using it to make something so bold and outwardly odd ... @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on display in his antic English dubbing for Miyazaki 's The Boy and the Heron ( 2023 ) , also gets another enthusiastic workout : with his squeaky , put-upon tone , Pattinson 's sad-sack of the clones is what Peter Lorre might have sounded like had he been reincarnated as an ' 80s high-school movie Poindexter . It checks out : the star says that he modelled the voices on ' 90s animation furballs Ren and Stimpy , themselves a riff on Lorre 's anxious stylings . <p> It 's a wonderful physical performance that culminates in an awkward threesome , with Nasha sandwiched between tag-Team Edward and Mickey 18 . In what might be the movie 's funniest moment , Mickey greases his finger and uses it to erotically tousle his doppelganger 's hair . Is Mickey 17 , to paraphrase Toni Basil , about to take it like a man ? <p> Tumblr slash fic aside , Mickey 17 does n't do much new with its clone concept -- more fun when Sam Rockwell was a lunar pilot arguing with multiple versions of himself in Moon ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which was so much more entertaining when Tom Cruise got stuck in an endless loop of death and rebirth in the sci-fi action thriller Edge of Tomorrow ( 2014 ) . " What does it feel like to die ? " everyone asks Mickey , but the movie is n't especially interested in exploring the answer , comedic or otherwise . <p> Bong 's movie is n't lacking for ideas , however borrowed most of them may be , but it never quite finds a groove . Coming from one of the 21st century 's most kinetic and consistently inventive filmmakers , an artist who thrives on the high-wire rush of the tonal swerve , that 's a surprise . Think of the rich emotional through-line that anchored the bleak horror , zany comedy and tenderness of Okja , or how Parasite -- which was so much more than catnip for class warriors -- inscribed all of its characters with empathy , rather than simply reserving its ire for the wealthy . <p> By contrast , the blustery Mickey 17 ca n't get its many tonal elements to gel . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ feeble eat-the-rich bits that feel like Saturday Night Live sketches . @@122298225 <h> Save articles for later <p> Some concepts in European languages are hard to translate . Some that we have n't even attempted to translate have become part of the English lexicon , like savoir faire , dolce vita and Zeitgeist . <p> But these notions are worth deciphering if you want to understand the native culture and blend in with locals . Better yet , they offer an alternative path to enjoying yourself beyond the well-worn tourist sights . <p> These nifty cultural concepts do n't need to be confined to their countries of origin . They might provide hints of how to travel anywhere , and how to free yourself from sightseeing duties which -- let 's admit it -- can get both tiring and tedious . So kick back , relax and get yourself into the European mindset . <h> Waldeinsamkeit in Germany <p> Breisgau in the Upper Black Forest . <p> What is it ? A solitary retreat to the forest for quiet contemplation of your life , which brings both comfort and perhaps a little melancholy . <p> Tell me moreWaldeinsamkeit saw a big revival @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forested , during the pandemic years as everyone sought calm in the woods , although it has its roots in the Romantic movement which first saw nature as being uplifting and liberating . Take a hike , ponder your life , and be aware of details such as moss , leaves and forest sounds . <p> Advertisement <p> Try it The Black Forest in south-west Germany , long associated with folk tales and cuckoo clocks , is n't all forest but has large tracts of fir , beech , birch and oak trees interspersed with lush rolling countryside . It has a good network of public transport and hiking paths . Mummelsee to Hornisgrinde is popular for its sweeping views and forest-ringed lake and is an easy four-kilometre trail . Baden-Baden Panoramaweg is also beautiful but a more challenging 45 kilometres , divided into four stages . <p> More Check into the Hotel Baren ( baeren-titisee.de ) in Titisee-Neustadt and enjoy the town and lake while also being on the forest edge . Wellness facilities provide relief after long walks . See hochschwarzwald.de <h> Sobremesa in Spain <p> Lingering over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is it ? Life is art in Spain . <p> Ideal spot for sobremesa ... Raimunda restaurant , Madrid . <p> Advertisement <p> Try it Heat-induced summer somnolence makes the afternoons in Madrid the place for long lunches . It 's hard to beat Plaza de Oriente , facing the royal palace and an equestrian statue surrounded by petunia beds . Plaza de Santa Ana is more laid back , with a buzzy local atmosphere . It remains packed long into the evening , so the truly indolent can stretch their sobremesa into tapas time . The 17th-century Plaza Mayor is sumptuous , but you 'll pay tourist prices . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lovely architecture , and leafy Plaza de la Paja . <h> Flanerie in France <p> What is it ? Idleness , especially aimless strolling in the streets ( seeing a pattern here ? ) . " Sauntering " might be the closest equivalent in English . <p> Tell me more The French have a whole philosophy on how to be a stylish flaneur . Aim for urban exploration without purpose and detached observation of street life . Do n't sight see , just soak up the atmosphere . Since flaneurs were associated with modernity in the 19th century , do n't confine yourself to old towns . <p> Parc de la Tete d'Or in Lyon is France 's largest public park.Credit : iStock <p> Try it Paris is the obvious choice , but sunnier Lyon , with its riverfronts , is made for loitering and does n't distract with too many dutiful monuments and museums . It has lively waterfronts , cafe-cluttered squares and parks -- Parc de la Tete d'Or is France 's largest public park -- and distinctive neighbourhoods , of which St Jean has wander-worthy French Gothic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's top gastronomic scene means lingering lunches accompanied by local Beaujolais are a must . Enjoy the sun on your face , the breeze , the whisper of leaves on trees . Forty-eight hours of proof that getting good information in 2025 is a disaster . <p> As a South East Queensland resident waiting for Alfred to cross the coast , my algorithm flooded me with relentless updates on the cyclone -- from everyone , for days . There was no hierarchy to what I saw . Media outlets , local government , the Bureau of Meteorology ( BoM ) , independent weather accounts , influencers catastrophising or downplaying events , TikTokers filming exploding powerlines and Brisbane residents packing emergency kits under sunny skies -- all competing for attention with equal weight . <p> A Weatherzone forecast of the wind Cyclone Alfred was expected to produce.Credit : Weatherzone.com.au <p> Everyone was tracking Alfred . Everyone had an opinion on its path . But with each update , I was no more informed . <p> On Friday , someone in my local community group posted a map showing the cyclone 's eye passing directly through my suburb . Like anyone could know that . It was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more intense than my cyclone experience . <p> By Saturday afternoon , Alfred had not yet crossed the coast . When it did , it was no longer a cyclone but still brought extreme winds , flooding rains and widespread power outages throughout Sunday . Authorities were right to warn the community . And had the storm moved slightly north or intensified , the impact could have been much worse for Brisbane . <p> Spectators battered by waves at Brunswick Heads.Credit : Nick Moir <p> But social media does n't reward measured warnings . The worst-case scenario always leads because alarmism feeds the algorithm . " She 's not alone in her belief . The Edelman Trust Barometer shows trust in journalists is at an all-time low , with 70 per cent believing they lie . Nine out @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . People caught in LA 's January wildfires struggled to get reliable emergency advice because misinformation ran rampant online , even fanned by the US president . <p> Loading <p> It was rife during Cyclone Alfred too : a fake video claiming to be footage of Brisbane enduring 220km/h winds @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ multiple images of the radar claiming to be evidence Alfred was engineered by humans ! <p> There was a time when you opened your newspaper and the most important stories were placed in order from front to back . @@122299737 <p> Political bipartisanship across successive Australian governments has overseen a massive expansion of oil , gas and coal production despite promises to act on climate change over the last three decades , a new report suggests . <p> The report , Exporting Harm : The Climate Toll of Australia 's Fossil fuel Expansion , by the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative , a diplomatic and civil society campaign to create a treaty to stop fossil fuel exploration , expansion and set up a managed phase-out of oil , gas and coal use , to examine Australia 's track record on climate change . <p> It found that despite its rhetoric , Australia has worked to establish itself as " a fossil fuel behemoth " over the past three decades since the International Panel on Climate Change released its First Assessment report in 1990 , with the country exporting increasing amounts of fossil fuels even as its domestic emissions have fallen . <p> In the fifteen years after the release of the First Assessment Report , the burden of Australia 's fossil fuel exports doubled . It doubled again between 2005 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and gas exports . <p> During this time the Australian government was variously led by both Labor and the Coalition , in what Michael Poland , campaign manager for the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative in Northern New South Wales said was " a bipartisan consensus on expanding coal and gas . " <p> " At least Russia is somewhat honest about being a major fossil fuel producer , " Poland said . " I think for me that fossil fuel exports have doubled twice in the past three decades really just shows how deeply ingrained bipartisan support for the fossil fuel industry is . <p> " Both major parties have had a bipartisan position on expanding oil and gas . In the wake of years of cyclones and floods and heatwaves , it 's really time to break that repetitive cycle . Built in prefabricated pieces , modular homes require less labour to construct , saving both time and money . <h> What is a modular home ? <p> Modular homes are prefabricated pieces of homes that are built in a factory to specific specifications . Factory production enables an almost complete product to be shipped to remote areas where trades and materials can be scarce . <p> This is particularly the case in regional areas where sourcing materials and labour @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This production method minimises material waste and increases efficiency , lowering the overall cost . <p> Modular construction is primarily defined by two methods : volumetric and panelised . Volumetric modular involves delivering a fully finished house directly to the site , arriving as a complete home on the back of a truck . <p> In densely populated urban areas , where access can be more limited , panelised construction is often the preferred method . This approach involves assembling pre-fabricated wall panels on-site , providing tradies with an increasingly popular flexible solution . <h> Why regional landowners are choosing modular <h> Price <p> Modular housing is noticeably less expensive than traditional homes are to build as there is far less labour and materials involved . <p> The cost efficiency of modular homes makes them a viable option for low-income families , seniors and others who may find traditional construction unaffordable . Additionally , faster build times can lead to reduced holding costs and capital . <p> Modular homes are especially attractive to community housing providers who look for low cost solutions to ensure affordable housing reaches those who need @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ advantages of modular homes is their ability to help address the growing national housing shortage . Built off-site in a controlled factory setting , modules can be constructed much faster than traditional homes , allowing for a quicker response to housing needs . <p> Traditional construction can take 12 months or more , whereas modular manufacturers complete projects in just 12 to 16 weeks . Once delivered , the structure can be assembled in just a matter of days . <p> The potential for modular construction to scale up and contribute to solving the housing crisis is immense . Especially as communities and governments look for innovative ways to meet the needs of a growing population . <h> Weather proof construction <p> Modular homes can be built regardless of weather conditions , avoiding delays common in traditional construction . <p> Globally , weather delays impact 45% of projects and with rising temperatures due to climate change on-site construction challenges are expected to increase . <h> Sustainability <p> As environmental awareness grows , regional Australians are prioritising sustainability in their home designs . The Australian government has introduced a few programs that together incentivise the construction of regional modular homes . <p> In addition to this some states also offer incentives to more sustainable energy efficient homes further leading customers to modular construction . <p> With the popularity increasing the appreciation of modular housing is also strong . @@122339038 <h> What Ferris Bueller has over Trump <p> There is a famous , contradictory adage , " We learn from history that we do n't learn from history " or , more generally , those who ca n't remember the past are doomed to repeat it . This is the case with Donald Trump and trade wars . This week , the United States president stunned his closest allies again with the imposition of 25 per cent tariffs on steel and aluminium , dashing Australia 's hopes of an exemption . This is only the latest move in America 's long and undistinguished history of trade wars and skirmishes . A reasonable adult might have expected the American president to have learnt from his country 's own history -- indeed , from his own historical experience with his trade war against China in his first term . <p> During his 2016 presidential campaign , Trump constantly referred to US trade with China , and the agreement that enabled it , as a primary cause of the loss of US manufacturing jobs and intellectual property . He said China was responsible @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ world " , focusing on the US trade deficit with China . He declared , " We ca n't continue to allow China to rape our country . " He pledged , as the " great dealmaker " , to cut a better deal with China that would help American businesses and workers compete . <p> In January 2018 , Trump initiated tariffs and other trade barriers on China , hoping to force changes in what he claimed had been " longstanding unfair trade practices and intellectual property theft " that had contributed to a trade imbalance favouring China . In response , China labelled the US as " protectionist " but responded with tariffs of its own . This tit-for-tat process of tariff increases persisted to the end of Trump 's first term , and the trade war was considered a failure for the US . Specifically , the US trade deficit with China continued to grow throughout 2018 , to a record level , despite Trump 's tariffs . The trade war caused economic pain on both sides and led to diversion of trade flows away from both @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ President Emmanuel Macron and Chinese President Xi Jinping signed some 15 trade deals , serving to increase pressure on Trump to also do one with China . <p> The economic consequences for the US were significant . US growth slowed , business investment froze and companies did n't hire as many workers . Many farmers went bankrupt and manufacturing and freight transportation were hit hard . Trump 's action amounted to one of the largest tax increases in years . Moody 's Analytics , in a study in September 2019 , found that the trade war had already cost the US economy nearly 300,000 jobs and an estimated 0.3 per cent of real gross domestic product . Other studies have put the impact on growth higher , about 0.7 per cent of GDP . A 2020 Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Columbia University study suggested US companies had shed a total of at least $1.7 trillion in value as a result of US tariffs imposed on China . Farmers lost the majority of what was once a $24 billion market in China as a result of Chinese retaliatory @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It is most noteworthy that while the US deficit with China decreased after 2018 , the overall trade deficit did not . Trump 's unilateral tariffs on China diverted trade flows from that country , causing the US trade deficit with Europe , Mexico , Japan , South Korea and Taiwan to increase as a result . <p> Trump 's successor , president Joe Biden , kept these tariffs in place and added a number of other levies on Chinese goods , especially electric vehicles and solar panels . However , since February 2025 , Trump has imposed a total of 20 per cent tariffs on China . This time China has retaliated with tariff increases on the US and by threatening the US with " any type of war " , which " it will fight to the end " . <p> If Trump is n't to learn from history -- and we can only assume this is the case -- perhaps he should catch a re-run of the 1980s cult movie Ferris Bueller 's Day Off , with its lesson on tariffs . <p> To recognise the futility @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the US experience in the 1930s , when the Smoot -- Hawley Tariff Act raised levies across the board -- to the highest rates since the Tariff of 1828 on more than 20,000 imported goods . This prompted retaliatory tariffs by many other countries and hurt the US economy , worsening the effects of the Great Depression , with a 67 per cent reduction of American exports and imports . The principal losers were workers and farmers , despite the promises of prosperity under the protectionist act . The reaction of Canada , then the most loyal of US trading partners , is instructive . It imposed new tariffs on 16 products that collectively accounted for almost a third of imports from the US and forged closer links with Britain and its empire , as well as France and a new relationship with Germany . The two politicians for whom the tariff act was named , senator Reed Smoot and representative Willis C. Hawley , lost their seats , and the swing in the senate in the 1932 elections was the largest in history -- equalled in 1958 and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ presidential campaign , when he was pledging the toughest tariffs in almost a century , The Economist magazine commented that " Smoot -- Hawley became synonymous with disastrous policy making " . It was so catastrophic for growth in America and around the world -- global growth fell by two thirds -- that legislators have generally been reluctant to touch the issue since . <p> This latest tariff episode belongs to a long history of protectionist policies in the US , stretching to the beginning of the 19th century . The American Civil War was partly triggered by a tariff debate . The southern , agricultural states opposed any form of protection , whereas the northern , industrial states wanted to protect their manufacturing base . I was interested to note in my recent reading of the ascendency of president Abraham Lincoln that he actually raised tariffs during the Civil War . From 1790 to1860 the average tariff increased from 20 to 60 per cent . The region 's national parks were closed after ex-tropical cyclone Alfred dumped more than 1100 millimetres of rain on the mountains and fierce wind gusts tore down trees and power lines , threatening the forest-dwelling communities that live there , and leaving them isolated and without power for several days . <p> After bunkering down through the storm , hinterland resident Steve Noakes returned @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ retreat that he chairs , on Wednesday to find significant storm damage . @@122341933 <h> On the ground in Alfred 's wake <h> Save articles for later <p> Add articles to your saved list and come back to them any time . <p> Advertisement <p> This time last week , like so many Australians , I watched transfixed as Tropical Cyclone Alfred edged closer to the coast of southern Queensland , threatening to devastate communities with 100km/h wind and flooding rains . <p> By the time the storm made landfall about 9pm on Saturday , it had lost some of its force while stalled off the coast and was downgraded to a tropical low . Mercifully , population centres in northern NSW and south-east Queensland still reeling from the 2002 floods were spared the worst . Many were still affected , however , as the storm carved a trail of destruction . <p> Although things could have been so much worse , this was still an important story for The Age to cover . <p> Beyond the immediate and distressing impact on local communities -- many of them with strong links to Melbourne -- Alfred will almost certainly drive up insurance premiums and has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ our homes . This is a prevalent issue in many Victorian communities , such as Rochester . <p> Loading <p> Crucially , it has also sharpened the nation 's focus on the very real cost of climate change . This , after all , was the first time a tropical cyclone had threatened Australia 's east coast this far south in more than 50 years , and experts warn we may see more , and more severe , extreme weather further south as our atmosphere and oceans continue to warm . <p> This is why The Age dispatched senior reporter Adam Carey and photographer Justin McManus to the Gold Coast this week to support our Brisbane Times colleagues and cover the unfolding story from the ground . In this week 's editor 's note , I thought you might like to hear from Adam about what he found and what it 's like to report on an event such as this . <p> Adam , where are you at the moment ? On my way home from Surfers Paradise , where Justin and I had been staying since Monday , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ murky waters of the Nerang River . <p> Advertisement <p> Can you describe the scene on the ground up there ? Post-cyclonic calm . Alfred has been and gone and most of the mess it left in its wake has been cleaned up . Surfers Paradise looks like a tourist town again , with all of its glitz , except for the inconvenient fact that the beach is gone , washed away by surging tides , and swimming in the ocean is banned . <p> Loading <p> How do you prepare for an assignment like this ? In this case , there was no time for planning . We got the call early on Monday afternoon and were on a plane by evening . Frantic packing yields interesting results . I packed two pairs of pants but no rain jacket -- heading into a tropical storm . <p> You were interviewing people who were probably at one of the lowest moments of their lives . How do you make sure you can tell their stories sensitively ? With empathy and a low-pressure approach . Ordinary people do n't need to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to share their stories if you do n't get in their face . If someone does n't want to talk or be photographed , we respect their wishes with good grace . <p> How would you describe the scale of the damage ? Tropical Cyclone Alfred lost intensity off the coast near Brisbane and was downgraded to a severe tropical storm by the time it reached the mainland . We 've seen property damage , some minor flooding and a lot of trees and powerlines down , but the scene is not one of devastation . <p> How are the locals holding up ? Alfred 's impact has been very unevenly felt . Up in the Gold Coast hinterland , entire townships lost power and were cut off from the rest of the world for days . We met a man who had just arrived home to find a tree had speared through his roof , and a single mother and her family whose home was flooded due to a leaking ceiling , who had to light a campfire inside their house for cooking . These communities had a strong @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we met , the storm seemed like little more than an irritant . One small business owner complained about the " overkill " of the government warnings and of having to close his business for a day during the height of the storm . <p> Is there a particular image or story that will stay with you after you return home ? The first look we got at the beaches of the Gold Coast were shocking , just to see how the ocean swell had carved these metres-high cliffs out of the sand and obliterated the beach . <p> Why is it important for The Age to cover a story like this , even though it happened almost 2000 kilometres away from Melbourne ? Many Melburnians have a connection to south-eastern Queensland . There are also important stories to be told about how forces of nature can upend people 's lives on a mass scale , whether close to home or not . Alfred is also an important climate story . It 's the first cyclone to travel this far south along Australia 's eastern seaboard in 50 years , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cyclones this far south with greater frequency . <p> How do you keep safe when covering extreme weather events such as this ? Heed the official warnings about where to go and where not to go . Stay in touch . And do n't be a cowboy . <p> Adam Carey is senior city reporter ( suburban ) . He has held previous roles including education editor , state political correspondent and transport reporter . He joined The Age in 2007 . Connect via Twitter or email .

@@122365909 <p> While some states , such as Victoria and the ACT , have taken steps to introduce minimum energy efficiency standards for rental properties , Australia as a whole still lacks comprehensive policies to address these issues . <p> Given the escalating impacts of climate change , rising energy costs , and the growing number of renters experiencing energy hardship , urgent reforms are needed to improve the quality and performance of Australia 's rental housing . <p> In this interview , Dr Sarah Robertson , Centre for Urban Research , RMIT University and Prof. Trivess Moore , Post-Carbon Research Centre , RMIT University , explore the key factors that contribute to poor thermal performance in Australian rental homes , the limited options available to tenants to improve their living conditions , and the policy changes required to ensure rental properties provide a comfortable and sustainable living environment . <p> Sarah Robertson and Trivess Moore : We know that the quality and comfort of housing in Australia is typically worse than what is delivered in many other developed countries , including our private rental stock . Australia was late to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Australia 's housing stock was built before the introduction of minimum energy efficiency requirements in 2003 through the Australian Building Code , now the National Construction Code . In Victoria , for example , a study found that the majority of homes built prior to the early 2000s perform at about 1.8 Stars , so not well ! <p> If zero stars is like being outside and 10 stars is living in a home that requires no mechanical or active heating or cooling to keep its occupants comfortable , 1.8 stars is a poor state of affairs . It means a house that is hard to keep warm in winter , and cool in summer , and large energy bills . <p> Research from 2008 that compared Australia 's 5-star standard with housing in the USA , Canada and the UK found that housing in these countries was significantly out-performing the then 5-star standard ( most states and territories now mandate 6 or 7 star minimum for new builds ) . <p> And other research has found that we 're also not building new dwellings to the standards that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to ensure that we do . <p> Increasingly developed countries are introducing or improving minimum performance requirements for private rental housing . There have been some policy changes in Victoria and the ACT to set minimum requirements for private rental housing but on the whole we need to do more to get private rental housing to a higher quality and performance standard . <p> Energy hardship is a real and troubling issue in Australia , with research suggesting that 40% of households who rent may be experience energy hardship , unable to heat/cool their home sufficiently or pay bills on time . <p> What are the key factors that make Australian houses , particularly rental properties , prone to overheating in summer ? <p> Multiple factors can play a role in a dwelling overheating . There are some really basic things which if missing can make a house really hot to live in during summer . This includes a lack of external shading to keep the sun out , the amount and type of glazing -- in particular our long history of using large single glazed windows means we have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ enter in summer . <p> Even things like the gaps and cracks around a leaky home or the colour of the roof can contribute . Dark colour roofs for example absorb a lot of heat . Insulation is also another key one but until the early 1990s there were no requirements for insulation at all ! <p> The external environment surrounding a home also contributes to how well it manages summer heat . What this means is that it is hard to keep the heat out in summer and occupants then have to rely on air conditioning to try and stay cool . <p> To what extent do current building regulations and energy efficiency standards in Australia address thermal comfort for renters ? <p> Australia has very few regulations to address thermal comfort for renters . Properties built more recently have to meet higher energy efficiency requirements under the NCC , but the majority of Australian housing stock was built prior to this , as I mentioned above . Newer 7 star homes will perform much better than older housing but will still not be comfortable all the time during @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ healthy indoor temperature . <p> Apart from the ACT , there are few minimum requirements for thermal performance of rental properties , and no disclosure of how a dwelling performs at the point of sale or lease . There is also no requirement to improve the quality and performance of existing housing . However , in other jurisdictions there are requirements to improve the minimum performance of rental housing such as in the UK . <p> What measures can renters take to improve the thermal performance of their homes - particularly if they are unable to make structural changes - and how effective are Victoria and the ACT 's minimum energy efficiency standards for rental properties in improving summer comfort ? <p> Although they are being discussed , in most states and territories there are no thermal performance standards for rental properties across Australia . Beyond temporary changes , tenants therefore have few opportunities to make changes to a property to improve its thermal performance . <p> If you live in the ACT , rental properties without ceiling insulation or insulation below an R-value of R2 are required to have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this requirement , but have not yet legislated it . In Victoria and Tasmania , there are minimum requirements for a fixed heater to be installed in one room , but this does n't include cooling . <p> In terms of what tenants can do , it is important to try keep heat out for as long as possible when it 's hot , so external shading , or if not internal shading , where that can be retrofitted will help . Fans are a good and low-cost option that provide a cooling effect . You can also get films which you place on a window which can give a double glazed window like performance at a much lower cost . However , renters are generally limited in what they can do with any permanent changes often requiring landlord approval . <p> If they feel comfortable , tenants could also speak with their landlord or real estate agent about having a Residential Efficiency Scorecard assessment or other energy efficiency assessment carried out . This is an appraisal of the home energy performance and comfort . Best to check your local @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and local councils also offer rebate programs for sustainability improvements for rental housing and you should explore what financial support might be available . <p> Minimum thermal performance or energy efficiency standards for rental properties and the disclosure of a property 's energy efficiency performance are important to raising standards and we have seen them work well in other locations . However , these need to be introduced to ensure housing unaffordability issues are not exacerbated . We also need to make sure that there is a strong retrofit industry which can deliver the right type of retrofits to improve outcomes for occupants rather than just what might be seen as ' easier ' or ' cheaper ' options . <p> How do factors such as urban heat islands and climate change exacerbate the issue of overheating in Australian rental properties ? <p> Climate change is seeing heat events last longer , happen more frequently and becoming more intense . For new builds , getting orientation right is a fundamental part of passive design . Depending on your climate , how a building is insulated and how , where and the type of glazing all play a role in how hot and cold a home gets without turning to active heating and cooling . <p> Are there cost-effective retrofitting solutions that landlords and policymakers should @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The best retrofit solutions for a property are tailored to that property and its local climate , so it 's best to get an independent energy efficiency/thermal performance assessment carried out , such as a Residential Efficiency Scorecard assessment . Local and state government often offer rebates on these assessments , so look out for these . <p> We know that as a general rule of thumb you will want to make sure you first seal up all gaps and cracks , then look at installing or improving ceiling , wall and floor insulation , ensuring good quality internal blinds and external shading devices ( including nature ) before thinking about some of the more costly actions like secondary or double glazing . <p> How do Australia 's rental laws and incentives compare to international examples where stricter energy efficiency regulations have been introduced ? <p> We know that there are some locations where there are requirements for rental housing to meet minimum performance requirements . @@122380546 <h> Judy Courtin The Catholic Church 's legal loophole for abuse <p> The decision in Bird v DP has the privileged , affluent and braggadocious church publicly thanking the High Court for a ruling that pierced the hearts of thousands of survivors who were , as children , raped or sexually assaulted by Catholic clergy . <p> The Bird who gave the case its name is Paul Bird , the current bishop of the Diocese of Ballarat in Victoria . <p> DP is the pseudonym of a man who was sexually abused in 1971 at the age of five by Father Bryan Coffey , the assistant parish priest at Port Fairy . <p> The Catholic Church insists that its clergy members are not employees . In Bird v DP , not only did the High Court agree with this , it held that the relationship between a clergy member and the institution is not even akin to an employment relationship . As such , the church can not be found liable for the sex crimes of its clergy members . <p> The Catholic Church chose not to accept the decisions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Appeal -- namely , that there did exist a relationship akin to employment between the clergy and the church . Instead of practising their teachings of compassion , they instead saw it as an opportunity to mount a complex legal challenge in the High Court . <p> The High Court relied on the black letter of the law and overturned the decisions of the lower courts . This decision means that thousands of survivors of Catholic clergy child abuse in Australia are denied justice . <p> Once again , the Catholic Church is getting away with it . In the eyes of the hierarchy , the church has been granted judicial approval to avoid its legal and moral obligations to right the odious wrongs of its criminal past . <p> The High Court decision has cleansed the Catholic Church with judicial absolution . No confession or penance is necessary for the institution that enabled the serious sexual offending of hundreds of paedophiles within its ranks , not even a mea culpa . <p> To fully appreciate the adverse consequences of this High Court decision , some context and history @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ requirements in an institutional abuse civil claim is establishing that the institution is legally liable for the crimes of the offender . <p> Once again , the Catholic Church is getting away with it . In the eyes of the hierarchy , the church has been granted judicial approval to avoid its legal and moral obligations to right the odious wrongs of its criminal past . <p> To establish such liability , there are two main legal hooks upon which we rely . <p> First is the law of negligence and second is the law of vicarious liability . <p> For an institution to be negligent , we must establish that not only did the institution have a duty to prevent reasonably foreseeable harm of the child but that the institution breached that duty . <p> Mostly , such a breach would involve the institution having prior knowledge of the offender but not acting on that knowledge . <p> We know from the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse that much " complaint evidence " was either destroyed or not documented in the first place . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , vicarious liability . This was at the nub of the High Court 's decision . <p> To prove vicarious liability , one must first establish that an employment relationship existed between the offender and the employer or institution . Second , the offender must have committed the crime " within the course of their employment " . <p> The Catholic Church in Australia argues that Catholic clergy are not employed . If they are employed by anyone , it is by God . <p> Up until 1999 , any teacher who sexually assaulted a child at a school was considered by the courts to be off on a frolic of their own and the employer could not be held vicariously liable . The sexual offending was not part of their role or duties as a teacher . <p> Since 1999 , common law countries such as Canada and the United Kingdom have expanded and evolved the breadth of vicarious liability by adopting policy considerations and employing a contemporary filter through which to view cases . These courts have kept up with a changing world . <p> In 1999 , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that if an organisation carries certain risks , the organisation should bear the loss if those risks materialise . In this case , a residential care facility for troubled children was an institution that " materially increased the risk of child sexual abuse " . That is , the concept of an " enterprise risk " entered the lexicon of vicarious liability law . <p> Three years later , in a UK decision that also involved troubled children in a residential care facility , the legal concept of a " close connection " between the offender 's duties or role and the sex crimes committed gained judicial approval . <p> Not in Australia , though . Despite the above advances , the High Court handed down a decision in New South Wales v Lepore , in 2003 , which did not accept that state school authorities could be held vicariously liable for child sexual abuse by teachers . <p> Back to the UK and the law continued to evolve such that , in 2010 , using the " close connection " test , it was found for the first time @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ crimes of its clergy . <p> In 2011 , developing these ever-widening concepts of vicarious liability , a UK court went further and established that Catholic clergy are in a relationship " akin to employment " . <p> In 2017 , Irish common law imposed liability on religious institutions by adopting the transatlantic concepts of " enterprise risk " and " close connection " and also found the relationship between the clergy offender and the institution to be one that is " akin to employment " . <p> Still not in Australia . <p> In 2024 , the High Court was asked , for the first time , to consider whether a Catholic institution could be held vicariously liable for the criminal actions of its priests . <p> The High Court grappled with the question of whether an employment relationship is a threshold requirement of vicarious liability . <p> Nowhere in the decision was there doubt that DP had been sexually abused . The judges were not considering that question and had no reason to disbelieve him . The only question was whether he should receive financial compensation for the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ response was " no " . <p> Had the same abuse been committed by a lay teacher , the church would have to pay . The special relationship between priest and God was the only way out . <p> The lone dissenter , Jacqueline Gleeson , described this critical case as " a missed opportunity for the Australian Common Law to develop in accordance with changed social conditions and in tandem with developments in other common law jurisdictions " . <p> Despite consecutive , congruent and sound legal developments elsewhere , Australia 's High Court instead handed down a retrograde judgement that only serves to protect the church 's assets . <p> The consequences of this decision are dire . <p> If a survivor can not prove the institution had prior knowledge of the offender -- an arduous and at times impossible challenge -- they face a legal dead end . <p> Instead of declaring the law on vicarious liability to be in line with the rest of the common law world , the decision of the High Court has survivors hopelessly disenfranchised . <p> Bishop Bird , who lauds @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to absolve his church of responsibility . The protection of the church 's assets clearly eclipses the needs of those children who were sexually assaulted . <p> In an effort to rectify this anomaly in the law , the High Court handballed the problem to the states and territories . <p> Legislation can and must reverse this High Court decision by retrospectively expanding vicarious liability to ensure institutions can be held accountable for the actions of priests , religious clergy and volunteers acting under the authority of the religious institution , regardless of prior knowledge . <p> It must also capture the actions of volunteers working under the authority of all institutions into which children are entrusted into their care . <p> Such legislation is urgent . <p> A third of the abuse survivors I represent are currently impacted by this decision . It is estimated there are about 2000 survivors in Victoria alone whose chances of a civil claim are currently nought . <p> Many of these clients ' claims will have been in the legal system for up to five years . <p> In a recent Victorian decision @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ grounds that the matter now relied upon anticipated vicarious liability legislation was denied . This person and potentially many hundreds of others with matters currently before the courts are being forsaken . <p> Trials listed before the date of any legislative reform may have to be discontinued . Justice will forever be denied . Such an outcome would be calamitous . <p> A priest can go into a family home to provide pastoral care , which is part of his job , and while wearing his clerical collar , rape a child in their own bed , and unless there is evidence of prior knowledge , there will be no justice . <p> A priest can rape a child in their own church , but without prior knowledge there can be no justice . <p> To rely on such a legal technicality to avoid responsibility is unconscionable , immoral and wreaks of greed and abject cruelty . <p> Remember , the Catholic Church insists its members are not employed -- unless , of course , it suits them . <p> During the pandemic , the Catholic Church successfully lobbied the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ religious organisations . By Ben Brooker . <h> MTC 's The Robot Dog is a thrilling step towards the future <p> What is it about robot dogs ? Pop culture abounds with them , from Doctor Who 's K-9 and the animated pooch of Hanna-Barbera 's Dynomutt , to the Wallace &amp; Gromit film A Close Shave , Battlestar Galactica 's Muffit Two and Sleeper 's Rags ( " Is he housebroken or will he be leaving little batteries all over the floor ? " ) . <p> Perhaps , as Virginia Woolf 's nephew and biographer , Quentin Bell , observed , " dogs are the fashion because we can fashion them to our will . Dogs , much more than cats , can be made objects of conspicuous leisure . " Cats -- solipsistic and self-sufficient , and by and large indifferent to the comings and goings of humans -- do n't lend themselves to robotic servility . <p> Lately , reality has tended @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in disturbing ways . Google " robot dogs " and you do n't have to scroll far to find headlines such as these : " Welcome to the Uncanny Valley : how creepy robot dogs are on the rise " and " Robot police dogs are on patrol , but who 's holding the leash ? " As I write , robotic dogs are guarding Trump 's Mar-a-Lago and locating Russian forces for the Ukrainian military . <p> The Robot Dog , a dramedy co-written by Hong Kong-born multidisciplinary artist Roshelle Yee Pui Fong and Luritja writer and technologist Matthew Ngamurarri Heffernan and presented as part of Asia TOPA by Melbourne Theatre Company , arrives amid a flurry of " robo-dramas " . Late last year saw productions of Jos ? Rivera 's Your Name Means Dream ( Melbourne 's Red Stitch ) and Amy Chien-Yu Wang 's AI May ( Brisbane 's Embodi Theatre ) , plays that delved into the evolving relationship between humans and machines . The Robot Dog most resembles the latter , its plot in fact almost a mirror image of AI May 's portrait @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ robot while also sharing its multilingualism and exploration of diasporic experience . <p> The Robot Dog points towards the future in more ways than one . Its interculturalism , reflected at every level of its conception and execution , is a breath of fresh air . <p> Fong and Heffernan locate their titular mutt somewhere between utopia and dystopia ( perhaps , to borrow Margaret Atwood 's useful neologism , it 's ustopian ) . Dog , as it ( she ? ) is simply known , is a Services Australia " old model guide bot " , part of a return-to-work mental healthcare plan in inner-suburban Melbourne , 2042 . It has blue " eyes " , a love-heart-shaped nose and a mouth that lights up while dispensing upbeat therapy-speak and Deepak Chopra quotes . <p> Dog 's previous owner , Wing Lam ( Jing-Xuan Chan ) , has died suddenly , and her unemployed daughter , Janelle ( Kristie Nguy ) , is tasked with sorting out her belongings or " assets " , in the neoliberal vocabulary of Hus , a sort of Google Assistant from hell @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ accompanied by her partner , Harry ( Ari Maza Long ) , a Luritja man striving for a promotion at the soulless corporation he works for . The play unfolds over the course of a week , each new day signalled by Hus 's passive-aggressive announcement of how many jobs Janelle must apply for along with unsolicited updates on the health of her stools . As Janelle struggles to cope with her grief , her mother makes occasional appearances in the form of a ghost bathed in shimmering pink light and dry ice , " like an echo " , as Janelle puts it , " from a singing bowl " . <p> If The Robot Dog has what dramaturgs like to call a central dramatic question , it might be whether AI technologies are more facilitative of human connection or alienation . In a sense , Fong and Heffernan 's answer is to place an each-way bet . Hus , the embodiment of a kind of soft despotism , suggests their belief in a Black Mirror-esque dystopia in which humans are endlessly surveilled and policed by intelligent machines . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Harry likens the effects of his " language augment " -- a piece of wearable tech reminiscent of Douglas Adams 's Babel fish -- to the effects of colonisation in how it forces alien words from his mouth , displacing the English that he has , ironically , been compelled to use for much of his life . <p> On the other hand , as Dog 's autonomy grows , fuelling both a rising rebelliousness and an inchoate spiritual awakening , its relationship with the oppressive Hus begins to deteriorate . @@122380574 <h> The destruction of more than 10,000 homes in the Los Angeles fires is a powerful reminder that Australia needs a total rethink of how and where we build to live . By Elizabeth Farrelly . <h> ' Country ' is a learning needed in Australia 's urban planning <p> Fires and floods . The message is getting harder to ignore , assiduously as we try . It is increasingly evident that nature has something to tell us . Something urgent . Basically , we 're not on top . <p> In Australia , whose edges we cling to like ants fleeing a hotplate , we 're hearing calls for a " managed retreat " from the coast . At the same time , increasingly destructive bushfires advocate a similar withdrawal from the bush . Then there 's all the floodplains we 've approved for development in recent years . Together , these climate-driven hints create a pincer movement , demanding nothing less than a total rethink of our settlement patterns and the precepts on which they 're based . <p> This shift , from colonial hubris to something softer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- is inevitable . What will it look like on the ground ? <p> The value of Australian coastal property at risk from sea-level rise and climate-driven storm surges is an estimated $26 billion . The risk from flood is greater still , with 953,000 homes -- 8.1 per cent of all properties -- under threat , with an estimated value of $768.5 billion . Both estimates are before we factor in lessons from Cyclone Alfred , but we know that tropical cyclones are becoming less frequent , more invasive and far more dangerous , with rainfall alone estimated to increase by 15 per cent per one degree warming . <p> Regarding fire , the risk is even greater . The 2024 Domain bushfire report estimates that 32,000 Australian homes ( 0.3 per cent of the total and valued at $31 billion ) are at high risk from bushfire . Overall , however , it notes , " Australia has around 5.6 million homes at risk of bushfire -- almost half of all properties nationally -- with an estimated value of $4.66 trillion @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fires , and the floods , are bonfires of our vanities . Moreover , both risks , the report notes , are " ever increasing " as climate change takes hold . What to do ? <p> January 's fires in Los Angeles destroyed roughly 11,200 buildings , most of them single-family homes . What needs to change ? <p> Architects , naturally , emphasise design . Therefore , he said , " it is primarily new homes that survived " -- those with no eaves , non-combustible roof and decking materials , no arbours , trellises , pergolas , carports , gazebos , vents or details that might trap windblown embers , and no nearby vegetation . <p> This is something of a tragedy for traditional LA architecture , distinguished as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these devices . @@122382766 <p> Firstly , it moved the wrong way . Most cyclones that form in the Coral Sea move east then out to sea by the time they get as far south as Brisbane . This one began on that trajectory , then turned around . <p> It also threatened to make landfall further south than usual . The last cyclone to get that close to Brisbane was Tropical Cyclone Wanda , which hit just north of the Sunshine Coast in 1974 . <p> Alfred also moved at a slower pace than your average cyclone , generating more damaging waves and washing away more sand from beaches in the process . <p> As global temperatures climb , scientists say some of the things that made Alfred unique could be a taste of the future . <p> So , could climate change one day send a cyclone as far south as Sydney ? And will such destructive storms become stronger or more frequent ? <p> Let 's look at what we do and do n't know about the future of cyclones in a warmer world . <p> Tropical Cyclone Alfred moved down @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ south-east Queensland . ( ABC News ) <h> Cyclones will become more intense <p> One thing all climate scientists agree on is that tropical cyclones will probably become more intense in the future . <p> To explain why , it might help to look at some of the ingredients you need to make a cyclone in the first place : <p> Warm water ( generally 26.5 degrees Celsius or more ) <p> What 's called " low vertical wind shear " ( that means pretty even wind speeds at different heights of the atmosphere -- if winds increase too rapidly with height , that can break up the circular motion of a cyclone while it forms ) <p> High humidity throughout the atmosphere <p> As global temperatures build , some of those ingredients are intensified -- essentially creating more fuel for tropical cyclones . <p> One of those ingredients is warmer water , says Mark Howden , the director of the Institute for Climate , Energy and Disaster Solutions at The Australian National University . <p> " Because of increased ocean temperatures , those cyclones that do occur are likely @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Professor Howden says . <p> " That 's because there 's more energy in the ocean , and so those cyclones , when they do form ... become much stronger , with higher wind speeds . " <p> It 's not just about the warmer water . A warmer atmosphere also helps add fuel to cyclones , says Kimberley Reid , a climate scientist with the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century at the University of Melbourne . <p> " As the atmosphere warms , it can hold more moisture , so that means when it rains , it will likely rain harder , " she explains . <p> On top of that , Dr Reid says , condensation ( the process of water vapour turning into a liquid , which is what happens when clouds form and rain falls ) is " exothermic " -- meaning it adds even more energy to the atmosphere . <p> That 's bad news because even small increases in wind speed mean big increases in damage . Wind 's power -- and potential to cause damage -- is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ if wind speed doubles , the damage it causes can increase eightfold . <p> Rising sea levels and higher rainfall mean we can also expect bigger storm surges and more coastal erosion from tropical cyclones , says Hamish Ramsay , a principal research scientist at CSIRO who specialises in tropical cyclones . <p> Some projections say cyclones will become less frequent , but stronger . Others say they will become more frequent and stronger . <p> " I think the key issue is we really need longer data sets to be able to make confident statements , and we 're dealing with something that happens a few times a year , so we 're not confident yet that these trends are necessarily going to continue , " Dr Reid says . <p> Despite the uncertainty over possible future frequency , Professor Howden stresses : " There is very little debate that , of the cyclones that occur , they 're likely to be considerably stronger than they have been in the past , and have all those other characteristics : higher peak wind speeds , more intense rainfall , more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ though tropical cyclones could become less frequent , the cyclone season could become longer . It comes down to that key ingredient again : warm water . <p> " With average sea surface temperatures going up , the threshold over which the temperatures go up in the summer period gets exceeded earlier on , " Professor Howden says . <p> " So the cyclone season extends , just like our fire season has extended here in Australia . @@122445695 <h> The five big policy challenges the next government must address <p> Elections are a time for policy ideas and policy vision to set Australia on a more prosperous path . <h> Subscribe now for unlimited access . <p> or signup to continue reading <p> All articles from our website &amp; app <p> The digital version of Today 's Paper <p> Breaking news alerts direct to your inbox <p> Interactive Crosswords , Sudoku and Trivia <p> All articles from the other in your area <p> As Australians prepare to go to the polls , Grattan Institute has been preparing a new book on the policies that should be on the agenda of whoever wins the 2025 federal election - Labor or Coalition , majority or minority . <p> Our new Orange Book - drawing title inspiration from the Red and Blue Books that the public service prepares for incoming governments - charts a path to improved living standards for all Australians , now and in the future . <p> Fortunately , Australia is not starting from scratch - progress is being made on several fronts , but the next federal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but difficult reforms , and tackle others that have been left in the too-hard basket for too long . <p> The 2025 election comes at a time of great uncertainty globally . And for many Australians , recent years have been hard . <p> Australians emerged from pandemic-era disruptions to find themselves in a cost-of-living crisis . With rising protectionist sentiment threatening global trade , the international rules-based order under siege , and the impacts of climate change showing themselves , is it really any surprise that fewer of us believe Australia is a land of opportunity , where hard work brings a better life ? <p> In this environment , it is easy to lose sight of the progress Australia has made . But we have made progress . Australia has navigated the crises of recent years while avoiding mass job losses and business bankruptcies . Australians are collectively healthier and wealthier than ever . And we are steadily reducing our carbon emissions . <p> With inflation having fallen , it is long-standing challenges that await , and we are better positioned than most countries to tackle them . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the next government will need to tackle the five big challenges we face : <p> Transitioning to net zero : we need to further bend the curve on carbon emissions , and focus on the economic transformation that accompanies decarbonisation . <p> Tackling the housing crisis : we need to relax planning constraints , boost supply , and support mobility . <p> Deepening talent pools : we need to improve our school systems , early childhood education , skilled migration , and delivery of human services . <p> Meeting the needs of an ageing population : we need to get better at tackling chronic disease and shore up sustainable retirement and aged-care systems . <p> Fixing the structural budget problem : we need to introduce bold tax reforms , implement sensible savings , make hospitals more efficient , and rein in NDIS costs to make the scheme sustainable . <p> None of these challenges is new . And in each case , Australia has already made a start . But the clock is ticking . <p> Productivity growth is the key to raising our living standards in the long term @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ levers , it can strengthen the foundations : a competitive economy , a well-functioning labour market , the conditions for people to flourish ( housing , health , education , and social cohesion ) , and the right infrastructure , tax , and regulatory settings . <p> Our Orange Book puts forward evidence-based policy ideas in all of these areas and more . <p> The transition to net zero will be easier with a predictable environment for investors and consumers . The next federal government should maintain the 2030 target , and set a 2035 target for emissions reduction of 65 per cent to 75 per cent below 2005 levels . Electricity and gas market reforms , and comprehensive industry policy , will also be needed for a successful transition . <p> Making housing more affordable is a social and economic imperative . There are substantial economic and budgetary benefits in halving the capital gains tax discount and curbing negative gearing , but boosting supply is the real game-changer for housing affordability . <p> While most of the levers sit with state governments , the federal government can sharpen states @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stamp duty for land taxes , and triple the Housing Australia Future Fund . <p> In health , chronic disease is the big system challenge . Australia must adopt a prevention agenda , alongside changes in how GP clinics are funded to support chronic disease management , and a greater focus on hospital efficiency , to help meet growing demand for care . <p> In education , we must lift our game to ensure the next generation of students gains the essential skills to thrive . Australia needs to set more ambitious targets for student <p> learning , and provide schools and teachers with the robust guidance , curriculum <p> materials , and professional development they need . <p> The NDIS provides life-changing support to many disabled Australians , but reforms to build up foundational supports and clarify eligibility for individualised support need to be implemented well to make the scheme sustainable . <p> There are also opportunities for the next government to improve our retirement incomes system by simplifying the system for retirees , curbing superannuation tax breaks that cost far too much , and strengthening the social safety @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ recommendations are major reforms , such as reducing income tax breaks , or broadening and raising the GST . Others are relatively easier , including staying the course on existing policies such as the Safeguard Mechanism and the New Vehicle Efficiency Standard to support the transition to net zero . <p> Some reforms would cost money , such as raising JobSeeker to a liveable level . Some would save money , such as counting more of the family home in the age pension asset test . Others would have very little budgetary impact but would improve confidence in our policy-making institutions , including reforms to reduce the influence of vested interests . <p> Governments have limited fiscal , workforce , and capability bandwidth , and that needs to be factored into the extent and timing of reforms . No government could implement all these reforms in a single term . <p> But if governments were to tackle a reasonable number of these reforms over the next decade , we would be well on our way to a more prosperous Australia . <p> Kate Griffiths is chief of staff of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ free at www.grattan.edu.au.
