@@122446851 <p> In a recent presentation , I recommended , quite unoriginally , that governments should have a greater focus on higher-impact , lower-probability climate risks . My reasoning was that current climate model projections have blind spots , meaning we are betting on best case scenarios . <p> Irresponsible at best and ' fatally foolish at worst ' , this approach is inconsistent with other security issues -- I do n't know many analysts assessing nuclear escalation or a potential Taiwan Strait crisis from the best-case angle . <p> Globally , January 2025 was the warmest January on record . This included severe heatwaves across Australia , with maximum temperatures as high as 17 degrees C above average . <p> This warming was unprecedented and , importantly , unexpected . This is an ever-increasing climate-related trend -- reality continues to outstrip scientific expectation . Given this , my use of the term ' lower-probability ' was itself , in hindsight , an example of this best-case mentality : designating high impact climate events as low probability is likely , at best , a dangerous underestimate . <p> Beyond blind spots @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ calculations and biases ) are not infallible . Therefore , the accuracy of probability estimates depends on the accuracy of the underlying logic . Regarding probability : <p> ... if climate modellers wish to determine the implications our greenhouse gas emissions will have ... their model/theory will not be adequate at predicting relevant system features at useful levels of precision and frequency unless it tells them the changes in the local temperature and precipitation . <p> Yet , current models seem unable to adequately predict global , let alone local , climate changes . In June 2024 , for the first time , global mean surface temperatures reached the Paris Agreement 's aspirational threshold of 1.5 degrees C of warming for 12 consecutive months -- again , much earlier than expected . <p> This is particularly concerning given that most climate impact research of the past decade has been based on temperature rises of 2 degrees C and below , this despite greenhouse gas trajectories setting the world on track to warm by more than 3 degrees C by 2100 . Various studies even suggest that we can not discount @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ drive the mismatch between warming estimates and research coverage . Firstly , as 2 degrees C is the benchmark of international targets , research likely reflects policy demand . Secondly , due to well-funded misinformation campaigns , scientists have been labelled alarmist and want to avoid such dismissal . Thirdly , the consensus process of the International Panel on Climate Change is inherently conservative , which also compounds the previous factors . <p> How can we deem potential climate impacts low probability if we have n't properly researched them and their potential dynamics under the higher temperatures we are headed towards ? <p> Further , we today are locking in the events that will undoubtedly happen tomorrow . This is often overlooked and underestimated by security practitioners -- unlike military conflict , for example , people are not fully in control . Feedback mechanisms exist within Earth 's systems that , once initiated by rising temperatures , will cause abrupt , self-perpetuating and effectively irreversible changes . <p> Thermal inertia reinforces this lack of control . The ocean stores more than 90 percent of Earth 's excess heat . Even @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ world would continue warming for at least another several decades as this stored heat is released . <p> Due to the factors outlined above , there is uncertainty regarding the reliability of probability estimates for specific events , when they might occur , and the chains of cause and effect that may trigger them . <p> However , uncertainty does not equal low probability . A lack of certainty around calculation inputs merely lowers confidence in the accuracy of probability estimates . Consequently , the actual likelihood of a particular event occurring may be much higher than predicted . <p> Moreover , given existing blind spots and biases , it is highly likely that probabilities around singular high-impact climate risks are underestimated , particularly within the security community . <p> If we analyse climate threats on a cumulative risk basis , the margin for error grows , increasing the collective probability estimates of climate events occurring . Hence , we can have confidence , given our current trajectory , that the collective probability of at least some high impact climate events materialising is high . We should n't use terminology @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ isolation and begin to better comprehend event compounds , cascades , and concurrency -- and fast . This is especially true for probability , as it informs much of the world 's risk and security analysis and management . <p> All trajectories are subject to change and human decision . But until this change happens , we are heading into uncharted territory . <p> We can , however , learn from another high-stakes area in which decisions rely on scientific evidence : public health . Patients are not treated by scientists undertaking clinical research , but rather by general practitioners . Justine Lacey and Mark Howden argue that a similar separation between scientist and practitioner would support better climate-science advice to policymakers . <p> This separation can facilitate relevant and targeted advice encompassing a range of views , largely independent of specific researchers . It could improve the interpretation and translation of advice , enhancing decision-makers ' understanding . This could reduce conflicts of interest and avoid narrowly informed and disciplinary-siloed advice . It would also create shared responsibility , alleviating pressure on the climate science community . <p> Although @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it -- to the benefit of probability estimates , decision-making and the public .

@@122472683 <p> Extreme heat is behind 7.3% of the heart disease burden in Australia , according to new research . This translates to an average of 49,483 years of healthy life lost to cardiovascular disease each year -- and this figure could more than double by 2050 . <p> Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death globally and in Australia , and it is sensitive to extreme heat . <p> " When the weather is hot , our hearts have to work harder to help us cool down , " explains lead researcher Peng Bi , environmental health expert from the University of Adelaide . <p> " This added pressure can be dangerous , especially for people with cardiovascular disease . " <p> These factors can worsen the symptoms of existing health conditions , from asthma to mental health to heart disease . <p> " Many of us have experienced how a warming climate can make us feel unwell , particularly during longer periods of extreme heat , " Bi says . <p> " However , it 's still not clear exactly how many people are living with serious heart @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we need to understand how this burden will increase in the future . " <h> Delving into the data <p> To begin to quantify this , Bi and colleagues drew on the Australian Burden of Disease Database to look at illness or death caused by cardiovascular disease . Focusing on a 15-year period between 2003 and 2018 , they applied a statistical model to determine how much of this illness or death could be attributed to heat in different areas of the country . <p> They found that over this period , Australians lost an average of 49,483 years of life each year to cardiovascular disease attributable to high temperatures . These are referred to as disability-adjusted life years ( DALYs ) . <p> Most of these years were lost due to death , not illness . The highest burden was in South Australia , while the lowest was in the Northern Territory . <p> But the team wanted to see how these numbers might change in the future -- which will depend on what actions we take now to eliminate fossil fuel emissions and reduce the future impacts of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we may take , they drew on two potential future scenarios used by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change : a pathway where emissions stabilise and Austrtalia 's annual average temperatures increase by 0.6-1.3 ? C by 2030 , ( Representative Concentration Pathway 4.5 or RCP4.5 ) , and a business-as-usual pathway known as " high emissions " where emissions rise , population grows , and there are no adaptation efforts ( RCP8.5 ) . <p> In both cases , the research found that there would be a steady increase in cardiovascular disease burden . <p> Under the RCP4.5 scenario , Australians will lose 90,779.7 DALYs due to heart disease caused by hot weather by 2030 , and 139,828.9 DALYs by 2050 . <p> Under RCP8.5 , the worst-case scenario , DALYs are projected to increase by to 95,343 by 2030 and 161,095 by 2050 . <p> This means the cardiovascular disease burden would nearly double , as compared to the current baseline . The Northern Territory will see the most significant increase , in terms of rate and proportion of the burden attributable to hot weather . <p> " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ population shifts , and adaptation strategies -- to give a full picture of the disease burden across Australia , " Bi says . <p> " This makes our study one of the first of its kind globally . " <p> Though the research is based on Australian data , its findings will also apply more broadly . <p> " While the specific risks may vary depending on local climates , population demographics and levels of adaptation , the overall trend -- that higher temperatures lead to more cardiovascular disease burden -- is likely relevant in many parts of the world , " Bi says . <h> Next steps <p> The most effective way to reduce the health impacts of climate change is to stop burning fossil fuels and begin the process to curb rising temperatures . <p> But the impact of hot weather on heart disease can also be significantly lowered using adaptation strategies . <p> These include individual measures like staying hydrated , remaining in a cool place and seeking medical help . However , adaptation strategies also need to be structural , as Bi and colleagues points out @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be related to socioeconomic status , financial support for cooling and subsidies for air conditioning/electricity costs may likely benefit those with fewest resources , " they write .

The outfit that 's doing most to alert us to the deep trouble we have with insurance is the climate campaigning Australia Institute . But when , sometime in the future , I decide you 're a bigger risk , it will be a different story . <p> Loading <p> The point is , there 's no magic in insurance . It can do the possible , but not the impossible . The way insurance works is that , if I can gather a " pool " of many thousands of home owners , each with only the tiniest risk of having their house burn down , I can promise all of them that , in return for a modest premium , they 're all fully covered in the event of a major mishap . <p> A few of them will have such a mishap @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of premiums and still have enough left to make it worth my while being in the insurance business . <p> Once the risk of your home coming to grief becomes less than tiny , however , the game changes . When more than a few people in the pool make claims , I make no profit , or maybe a loss . So I can start by making owners with bigger risks pay more than those with low risks , but once your risk is too high , I can either charge you a premium that 's impossibly high , or just refuse you insurance . <p> Because of their ever-growing record of claims , the insurance companies are well-placed to make a reasonably accurate assessment of how risky it is to cover your house -- even to the point of charging more in some parts of a suburb than others . <p> This means , of course , that home owners in some parts of the country will be charged far more than others . Premiums will be highest in northern Australia , where cyclone risk is higher , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . And even people living well away from harm in the inner city will be paying more to help out . <p> Loading <p> All this is why we should be doing more -- and have been doing more this long time -- as our part in the global effort to limit climate change . But what should we do to reduce the damage that 's arrived or is on its way ? <p> Well , certainly not having the government subsidise insurance . That would just encourage people to keep doing what they should stop doing . Taxpayers ' money should be used only to help people get away from the risk of fires and floods . <p> Just as fighting a fire is easier than fighting a flood , bushfires are less difficult to get away from than floods . We must start by preventing anyone else building in risky areas . <p> Then we need to move people off the flood plain . As for Lismore , the whole town needs to be moved to higher ground . <p> But here 's a tip . Do n't @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these issues in the election campaign . That 's not the way losers behave . Much easier to shift the blame to the greedy insurance companies .

@@122487692 <h> How to Calculate How Many Solar Panels You Need to Charge Your EV <p> You can harness the power of the sun 's rays to charge your electric vehicle . Here 's how many solar panels you 'll need to do it . <p> Charging your electric car at home will only increase your electric usage unless you add another renewable energy source , such as solar panels , to offset it . <p> Getty <p> Driving an Electric vehicle is one way to help reduce the impact you have on the planet , but did you know that you can take things a step further , too ? Your EV will inevitably need to be charged at some point , and that means plugging it into your home to add some electricity to those batteries . The best way to charge your EV is by using renewable energy to power your home 's EV charger . One popular option is to use solar panels to power your home and your vehicle -- and sometimes you can even sell the excess power back to the grid , too . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ undeniable that EV charging stations are becoming the norm . Automakers are making headlines as they invest in new EV technology , and efficient solar panels installed on rooftops are also becoming commonplace . <p> Can solar panels save you money ? <p> Interested in understanding the impact solar can have on your home ? Adding solar panels to the equation adds even more layers of complexity to an already significant investment . <p> Here 's what you need to know about powering your home and EV with solar panels , and how many panels you 'll need if you go that route . <h> Why use solar panels to charge an electric vehicle ( EV ) ? <p> There are some less @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ free , clean electrons pulled from the sky streaming into your car 's battery . <p> Most home EV chargers treat your car like any other appliance that needs to be plugged in and charged overnight . Actually , it 's more like a quite needy appliance that requires a particular current ( DC ) and lots of it as quickly as possible , which can mean operating at high voltage . <h> Considering Solar Panels ? <p> Our email course will walk you through how to go solar <p> By signing up , you confirm you are 16+ , will receive newsletters and promotional content and agree to our Terms of Use and acknowledge the data practices in our Privacy Policy . You may unsubscribe at any time . <p> As Wyldon Fishman , founder of the New York Solar Energy Society , explained , solar panels and electric vehicles both operate with direct current ( DC ) , meaning there 's no need to install an inverter between your panels and EV , although a charge controller is still imperative to have in the circuit . DC can also run at lower , safer voltages . <p> Relying on solar panels rather than the grid to charge your electric vehicle also means not having to worry about being stuck at home with a dead battery if the power goes out , especially if you opt to pair your panels with a battery or other solar storage . <p> A home 's energy set up @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and an EV charger . Depending on the consumption , size , efficiency and how many panels you get , this equipment could accommodate all or some of this home energy production . <p> Getty <h> How much energy is needed to charge your EV at home ? <p> First , consider your goals for your solar charging system . Do you want to charge your car using your solar panels , and will you primarily be charging overnight ? If so , you 're going to need to install a battery or other storage system . <p> In most cases , you 're likely to have a solar system that 's hooked into the grid as well as your home , perhaps with a connected battery for emergency backup , or not . <p> If this is your scenario , it could be helpful to know how much of your existing solar output the rest of your home is consuming . If you never pay a utility bill or your utility bill is primarily for nighttime or cloudy days ( when your solar panels are n't at work ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more than you need and the extra is being fed into the grid or a battery or both . Some of this excess energy could be used to charge your EV , meaning you will need fewer solar panels to drive a fully solar-powered car . <p> Once you 've got an idea of whether you 're running a solar surplus , the next step is determining how much additional demand an EV will add to your system . <h> How many solar panels will I need to charge just my EV ? <p> First , consider how much you typically drive in a day . Put simply , the more you drive , the more wattage you 're likely to need in panels . <p> Here 's the steps to figuring out how your average daily energy needs to power an EV . <p> Step 1 . Determine how many kilowatt-hours your EV uses per mile . The EPA and US Department of Energy 's fueleconomy.gov site lists the estimated efficiency of all electric cars in kWh per 100 miles ; simply divide by 100 for a per-mile estimate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by the number of miles you anticipate you drive on an average day . ( You can get your average daily miles by observing your driving habits for a few days or by dividing your annual observed mileage by 365 ) . This gets you the total number of kilowatt-hours you 'll need to produce to power your daily driving . <p> Step 3 . You can then divide the EVs needed kilowatt-hours by the number of peak sun hours you can expect to receive at your location each day . <p> Step 4 . The final figure should give you the size of your ideal EV-charging solar array in kilowatts . <p> Step 5 . We will use a solar panel wattage of 410W , such as the Q.PEAK Duo Black from Qcells , to calculate the number of panels needed for the Hyundai Ioniq 6 . Convert the 410W to kilowatts by dividing by 1,000 ( 0.41 kW ) . <p> In this example , six Qcells solar panels are needed to accommodate the energy needs of the Hyundai Ioniq 6 with average driving habits . You can also build a stand-alone off-grid system that 's dedicated to just your car . <p> Fishman recommends building a carport topped with solar panels at just the right tilt to get a good amount of sun on average , based on your location on the globe . <p> " A carport is fixed at latitude , " she explained . " <h> Which comes first : A solar panel or EV purchase ? <p> If you 're dedicated to renewable energy and kicking fossil fuels to the curb , it makes sense to have your solar system all setup before you spring for the EV so you never have to worry about charging your car from dirtier energy sources that mix with renewables on the grid . <p> But the reality for many people will be that an EV and home solar energy are two very costly investments . A car or EV tends to be a personal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ whereas energy is a readily available commodity that we tend to think about less . So it would n't be surprising for people to prioritize a flashy new EV over adding solar panels to a home that already has access to electricity via the grid . <p> Ultimately , it comes down to your priorities and your situation . Maybe your utility is good about incorporating solar into its energy mix via its own solar farm systems , renewable energy credits or offering a community solar program . That means loading up batches of fries in a single layer and leaving just a little space between each piece if possible . The result is tastier fries in a shorter cooking time . <h> 4 . Shake for even cooking <p> Shake a few times during cooking for an even browning . <p> David Watsky/CNET <p> Halfway through the cooking time , pull out your air fryer 's basket and give it a good shake . It might surprise you to know that only four ( of the world 's 18 ) species of penguin live in Antarctica . Penguins are the poster fauna of the Southern Hemisphere , even though Gal ? pagos penguins scoot across the equator now and then . Species are scattered across the south , but only a few inhabit the Antarctic continent . The emperor and Ad ? lie penguins are endemic to its waters , while the Ad ? lie 's close relatives the chinstrap and gentoo penguins are found at many other southern hemisphere islands as well as Antarctica . <p> Ad ? lies penguins . Credit : Ian Connellan <p> Agus whet our appetites for penguin knowledge early in the voyage during an ' enrichment lecture ' in Scenic Eclipse 's state-of-the-art theatre . He explained that penguins get their collective name from the great auk ( Pinguinus impennis ) , which inhabited the North Atlantic until driven to extinction by humans in the mid-19th century . Although barely related to penguins , the flightless auk resembled them both in appearance and behaviour ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ late-16th century European explorers that first encountered penguins named them for the auk . <p> " So , if you have to survive such a difficult environment as this with cold weather and wind and snow , of course you need good thermal regulation , " Agus says . " If you 're naked in Antarctica you 're not going to survive for long . But penguins survive here in the water most of the year . " <h> How penguins survive in these harsh conditions <p> Penguins have three layers of thermal protection . First , their uropygial layer of feathers forms a waxy , waterproof exterior , which must be constantly maintained by preening with oily secretions from the uropygial gland near the tail . <p> Beneath the waterproof feathers is a layer of various types of downy feathers that traps air near the skin . And finally skin and body fat -- blubber -- form the ultimate seagoing insulating layer when at last water pressure pushes out the trapped air . The ' true ' Antarctic penguins -- the emperors and Ad ? lies -- have skin @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> After Agus 's lecture , we could n't wait to meet them ! And meet them we did : at least , we met Ad ? lies ( Pygoscelis adeliae ) , on our first peninsula Zodiac excursion , at the Madder Cliffs on the western end of Joinville Island , which is nearly the northernmost tip of the Antarctic Peninsula . <h> Ad ? lies penguins and other southern birds <p> The Ad ? lies and other bird species -- including Antarctic shags and various predators including skuas and giant petrels were massed on shore around the bay -- but it was their presence in the water that was most alluring . On land , they move comically ( a trait shared with other penguins ) and slowly . But they 're natural swimmers , and ' fly ' through the water at about 8 km/h , and nearly double that when they 're pursuing prey -- mostly krill -- or dodging predators such as leopard seals or killer whales . When they 're chasing food , Ad ? lies regularly dive to about 150m , and they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hold their breath for up to six minutes . <p> Adelie penguins on iceberg in Antartica . Credit : Getty . <p> You would n't describe Ad ? lies as small birds . Adults are around 70cm tall and weigh in the 4 -- 8kg range ( think about it next time you buy a decent-sized chicken to roast ) . They 've certainly got a bit of small-bird syndrome with a matching temper , and have been recorded muscling up to large predators like giant petrels . Perhaps they 're eternal teenagers ? That 's certainly what they look like when they 're lined up at the water 's edge , waiting for someone to jump in first ( and thus be the crash-test potential prey for any passing marine predators ) . <p> Their delightfully Francophile name comes courtesy of French explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville , who named them after his wife Ad ? le after first seeing them in 1840 . <h> What do you call a group of penguins ? <p> We saw Ad ? lies in large groups -- we decided the appropriate collective noun @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and had no hope of telling males and females apart . They 're about the same size and look much alike : a classic , out-of-a-picture-book tuxedo-clad penguin . Their white-ringed eyes stand out a little googly-eyed from black heads , and their white chests and bellies provide excellent camouflage against marine predators looking up from below to the water 's surface . <p> Incredibly , these dapper little seabirds are left in creches in their breeding colony when only 3 weeks old . Both parents go to sea to collect food for their chick ; they stay out for up to three days and might go as far as 120km offshore . Racing to beat the fast-closing cold , chicks go to sea when they 're only 7 -- 9 weeks old . Most wo n't come back again , to the same colony , until they 're old enough to breed at 3 -- 5 years old . <h> Chinstrap penguins at Palaver Point <p> A few days later and further south , at Palaver Point on Two Hummock Island , we have the privilege of kayaking among @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ flying ' through the icy sea as they forage . A place name including the word Palaver gives away an important fact about penguins : these are not silent animals . A penguin rookery is as noisy as an unsupervised primary-school class . <p> Chinstrap penguins in Antartica . Credit : Johnny Johnson/Getty . <p> That afternoon at Hydrurga Rocks ( named for the leopard seal -- Hydrurga leptonyx ) , we met the chinstraps afoot . The rookery was a lively place . Chinstraps loped to and from the water along ' penguin highways ' in their odd , swaying gait ; mating pairs called to each upon reuniting -- it was quite a din . <p> Chinstrap penguins ( Pygoscelis antarctica ) get their name for the narrow band of black feathers that extends from ear to ear below their chin and the cheeks -- just like a helmet chinstrap . They 're a similar size to Ad ? lies -- and like Ad ? lies , males and females look similar . They also have the same black-and-white , dressed-for-dinner look that 's effective camo against marine @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ chinstraps ' signature moves : they like to toboggan on land -- propelling themselves forward using their feet and flippers while lying on their stomachs . They 're also renowned for jumping over large distances and we spent several happy minutes watching a group returning from sea jumping their way back to their nests . <p> Chinstraps share with Ad ? lies a trait biologists call " site fidelity " : they invariably return to the nesting site where they were raised when it comes time to breed ( at 3 years of age ) ; it 's believed generations over thousands of years may have followed this habit . They build nests out of stones , and pebble stealing -- taking a stone from a neighbour 's nest and adding it to their own -- is a common sport , and the source of much rookery unrest . They generally raise two chicks each summer -- other penguin species feed the stronger of their chicks preferentially -- after a month-long incubation period that 's shared between males and females . <p> Their breeding colonies are mainly found on the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ enough south that persistent sea ice can upset breeding some years . Chinstraps leave their breeding colonies during March -- May to move north of the pack ice for the winter , and generally return to their colonies in October -- November . <h> The genuinely weird trait of chinstrap penguins <p> A recent research paper in Science has discovered that chinstraps have a genuinely weird trait : they accumulate about 11 hours of sleep daily by taking more than 10,000 four-second microsleeps . The nesting adults certainly looked like they were resting up after feeding at sea -- where they hunt for fish and krill -- but we could n't pick a micro- from a macrosleep . <p> On Hydrurga a snowstorm gradually increased in tempo , and the sight of chinstrap penguins going about their business against a backdrop of glaciated mountains , icy oceans and snowfall is one of our most enduring memories of visiting Antarctica . Life in the freezer indeed . <h> Gentoo penguin rookery , a sight <p> Christmas Eve was the day we got to walk on the Antarctic continent ( rather than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Neko Harbour , on the Graham Land coast , site of a large gentoo penguin rookery . <p> A Gentoo penguin in Antarctica . Credit David Merron/Getty . <p> The gentoo ( Pygoscelis papua ) is the second largest Antarctic penguin -- after the emperor -- and the third largest overall ( the king penguin , which breeds on subantarctic islands , is also larger ) . Gentoos grow up to 90cm tall and can weigh more than 8kg ; their penguin superpower is swimming -- they 're the fastest underwater swimmer among penguins , and can reach speeds over 30 km/h . They 're also more opportunistic than Ad ? lies and chinstraps when it comes to diet -- yes , krill and fish , but many other marine creatures as well -- which gives a clue to how they 're going in comparison to the other Antarctic penguins . <p> " We 're seeing that gentoos are actually expanding their population range in the western Antarctic peninsula , " Steve Forrest told the audience during a later enrichment lecture . " The Ad ? lies and chinstraps are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ because of their site fidelity , Adelies and chinstraps are just trying to stick it out in those same nesting spots ... and it 's just not working out for them in this changing environment . " <p> They also have another critical behavioural adaptation . " They 're more likely to re-lay , " said Steve . " So when we get those big random dumps of snow during the breeding season that really affects these other species , and nests are lost due to the eggs getting wet , gentoos can re-lay ... their eggs . The other two species are very unlikely to do that . " <p> With just the hint of a smile , he added : " We call that gentoofication . " <p> Trio of Gentoo penguins resting on sea ice in Antartica . Credit : David Merron/Getty . <p> Like their Ad ? lie cousins , gentoo behaviour often points them toward the teenager class . At Neko they have a beach to enter the water from , rather than launching off an ice shelf , and they 're particularly teen-like at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ water and appear to be contemplating the temperature . Or perhaps they 're thinking about food -- which , like so many things in Antarctica , is n't as straightforward as it appears . <p> As with other penguins and marine bird species , the gentoos ' diet is high in salt -- not surprising given that they feed on prey that 's about as salty as seawater . High salt concentrations in the body can cause problems , especially for chicks , so gentoos and other seabird species have a salt gland in their head that converts concentrated sodium in the body into a highly saline solution . This liquid concentrate drips out from the tip of the beak -- a nifty adaptation that allows gentoos and other penguins to survive without fresh water . <h> Searching for an Emperor penguin colony <p> It was Boxing Day , and our last full day in Antarctic waters after an incredible 12 days at sea on board the Scenic Eclipse . Credit : David Merron/Getty . <p> When we 've been stationary for perhaps an hour the voice of lead expert Discovery Leader , Helena Schofield came on the PA : a sole emperor penguin had been seen off the port side . <p> The bird enthusiasts on board grabbed their cameras and complimentary binoculars and raced outside -- if they were n't , like us , already there . They 're the biggest penguin species at up to ( sometimes exceeding ) 1m tall and weighing 40kg or more . King penguins stretch towards emperors on one measure ( they 're 80 -- 90cm tall ) but at 10 -- 15kg on average they 're well behind on body mass . But it is n't just about size . <p> Alone among Antarctic animals -- all animals , not just penguins -- emperors breed during the bleak winter months . They 're uniquely adapted to survive in places where temperatures can drop to -50 ? C and winds can reach 200 km/h . Unlike most penguins they 're social creatures , and they huddle together to keep warm -- a key survival behaviour . Because they huddle , they do n't spend energy defending territory . They 're the only penguin species that 's not territorial . <p> On the physiological side , they have large reserves of energy-giving body fat ( hence their hefty weight ) and their activity is limited during winter . Relative to their size , their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and their several layers of scale-like feathers are n't ruffled until winds blow past 110 km/h . They have special chambers in their noses that save much of the heat that 's normally lost exhaling breath , special fats in their feet that stop them from freezing , and unusually strong , ice-gripping claws . <p> Our emperor visitor seemed to be feeding . It periodically appeared in an ice-free pool , then disappeared underwater for several minutes , before popping up again . Just the distant sight of it caused outbreaks of smiles . <p> Emperors incubate their eggs through the depths of the Antarctic winter . Females lay a single egg in May or June , then the males take over and incubate the egg in a special brood pouch -- carefully keeping it off the ice -- for the next nine weeks , while their mates are feeding at sea . The males do n't eat for even longer than that ; it could be as long as four months -- from when they arrive at the colony to breed , through incubation , egg hatching and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ body weight falls away through this period . It 's the body fat reserves that they built up during their summer feasting that keep them alive . <p> And what a feast ! Through summer emperors gorge on krill , Antarctic silverfish and other fish species , and some squid species . An adult emperor consumes about 2 -- 3 kg per day on average , and up to twice that on a bumper day . While they 're feeding they demonstrate why they 're the penguin-class diving champions . They generally hunt food at 150 -- 200m depth , but the deepest emperor dive recorded is 565m . They usually stay submerged for 3 -- 6 minutes but can go much longer -- the longest recorded dive is 22 minutes . <h> Emperors under threat <p> Given all that 's amazing about emperors , predictably there 's some bad news : these giants of the penguin world are the species perhaps most threatened by climate change . The IUCN moved emperors from their list of least concern to the near threatened list 2012 ; the main risk they face @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ change . But overall numbers are for the moment only dropping slightly , and for reasons not entirely clear , as a 2024 study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B reported . <p> Certainly , isolated climate events can have a big impact . In spring 2022 , record low levels of sea ice in the western Antarctic Peninsula led to a " catastrophic breeding failure " of the region 's emperor penguins , according to a study published in 2023 in the Nature journal Communications Earth &amp; Environment . <h> Climate change risk for Antarctica and its penguins <p> " This is what we do know for sure , " Steve Forrest told us . " Temperatures in the peninsula have been going up dramatically over the last several decades -- year-round a 3 ? C change . <p> " This is a dramatic , impactful , change and in the peninsula we 've been seeing it in terms of the reduction in glacial mass , reduction of sea ice annually , and that affects kind of everything that happens here . " <p> For now the effects @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as Oceanites ' long-term census work indicates , things are changing . <p> " Penguins are long-lived species , so they can give us a good idea of what 's happening in a climate from year to year and decade to decade , " said Steve . " We study penguins because they 're central to the food web . Penguins ' health tells us something about their predators , the whales and seals , and of course their breeding success tells us about the things that they prey upon , so the fish , the squids , and most importantly , of course , the thing they eat the most -- the krill . " <p> From the deck of a cruise vessel that 's close to land in the Antarctic Peninsula , you do n't need to be reminded of penguins ' centrality here . Cast your eyes around and you might see whales , or seals , or a bird in flight . By Lucianne Tonti . <h> Martin Grant : Australian fashion 's quiet achiever <p> Martin Grant may be one of the most successful fashion designers in Australian history , but he is not a household name . Despite the acts of heroism and kindness , we failed in one critical area . <p> We did n't speak up against selfishness and ignorance . Now we 're living with the consequences . <p> I glimpsed it one morning when a frail woman on a walking frame was brutally shouldered aside in one of those frenzied scenes in a supermarket toilet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ no one seemed outraged or surprised . Then came those who deliberately flouted lockdown rules . We did n't call them out enough . Soon after came the fights over masks and restrictions . And then the anti-vaxxers found their voice and a growing following . <p> The COVID pandemic tested us in many ways . Picture by Brendan McCarthy <p> What began with minor grumbling about personal freedoms and mounting scientific scepticism became a full-throated roar of defiance that did n't quieten but grew louder . Anti-vaccine sentiment slipped into the mainstream , hooking up with its troglodyte relative , climate change denial . <p> Science is now only " one side of the story " . No coincidence Australia 's childhood vaccination rates are declining as Robert Kennedy jnr , a man with a toddler 's grasp of science , becomes the world 's most powerful health official . <p> Anti-vax sentiment spilled into other areas . Distrust of experts soon became distrust of anyone different . Immigration , once a topic debated with nuance , is now declared the root cause of crime and social decay . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The loudest voices are drowning out the whispering of the sensible . <p> That 's the character test we failed . We excused the selfish and the ignorant because it was inconvenient and uncomfortable to challenge them . We allowed misinformation to thrive rather than confront it . <p> It 's the enduring lesson of COVID . Selfishness never stays small . Left unchecked it grows until personal defiance insinuates itself in public policy . <p> If you still cling loyally to science , many studies have exposed how extremists exploited the pandemic to normalise their messaging . <p> One , by the American University , highlighted the way extreme groups leveraged increasing distrust with government and traditional authority to spread misinformation , conspiracy theories and scapegoating . An Oxford study last year also linked the surge in extremism during COVID to the rise we now see in anti-Semitism , Islamophobia and xenophobia , while a report commissioned by the UK government underlined how hate groups exploited the pandemic to advance their racist platforms . <p> We did n't speak up loudly enough . We were too complacent - afraid @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Now the indecent , having used the cloak of the pandemic , are emboldened . " <p> Each battery delivered what the team described as " significant differences " in the speed at which the battery charges or discharges relative to its maximum capacity . <p> Similarly , the researchers conclude that the " main difference between the Tesla 4680 cell and BYD Blade cells is their formats : BYD uses a large prismatic cell format , while the Tesla 4680 cell is a large cylindrical cell with a significantly lower volume . " <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the way they connect their thin electrode foils , which the researchers believe is done with laser welding ( Tesla ) or a combination of laser and ultrasonic welding ( BYD ) . Their research reveals more about what to expect as earth 's glaciers and icecaps melt in the face of climate change . <p> Looking back helps us prepare for what 's coming -- the inexorable rise of the tide . <p> Our distant ancestors lived and hunted and survived the last great ice age -- the Pleistocene -- which started about 2.6 million years ago and ended around 11,700 years ago . At about that time , ice sheets covering much of Asia , Europe and North America stopped their advance . Why this happened is uncertain , but it may have been that the Earth 's tilt changed , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Lead author , Dr Marc Hijma and team looked at sediment cores from the North Sea , off the Netherlands , Germany and Denmark . These cores were from now-submerged Ice Age coastal wetlands ; so much water was caught up in ice back then , that sea levels were around 122m lower , globally . <p> As the ice melted between 11,000 and 3,000 years ago , the North Sea reclaimed those marshes . The now-flooded wetlands became buried in brackish and marine sediments , forming a 10-30cm layer of decayed organic matter -- compressed to ' peat ' by the increasingly deep mud . <p> It was a treasure trove of plant material awaiting a sediment corer . <p> The cores revealed the paleoenvironment before submergence , says Hijma , signalled by the types of microalgae ( diatoms ) and other plants . Different diatom communities form , depending on where they are in relation to sea level , which means that height above sea level could be worked out . Radio carbon dating gave sea level changes over thousands of years , and X-ray fluorescence analysis @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that sea level rise happened twice . The first about 10,300 years ago , was fast , at about 9mm per year , similar to that expected under the high greenhouse gas scenario for present-day climate change . The second , about 8,300 years ago , was slower -- about 8mm per year , and Hajimi , says was triggered by the release of meltwater from huge glacial lakes that formed at the bases of the melting ice sheets . <p> Sea level rose almost 40m , higher than a 10-storey building , until about 3000 years ago . <p> Hijma says that the study will help policymakers and scientists better understand what to expect , and to prepare , as the earth 's icesheets and glaciers melt , driven by anthropogenic climate change . Impacts in the now much larger human population will be orders of magnitude more severe than those our Ice Age ancestors faced , given 15% of Anthropocene humans live in fixed infrastructure near the coast -- 87% in Australia .

That 's the business of participants in this conference . <p> Two clear minds , Frank Knight in the US and John Maynard Keynes in the UK , defined uncertainty and risk for us a bit over a century ago . Risk is the unknown outcome from a known probability distribution . We do n't know whether any throw of two fair dices will add up to 3 or 11 . But we know fairly closely how many times we will see 3 or 11 if we throw the dice a thousand times . <p> Uncertainty is when we have no basis for knowing the probability distribution of possible outcomes . The US Defence Secretary in the George W. Bush administration made the concepts famous by referring to known and unknown unknowns arising from the invasion of Iraq . <p> When societies and polities receive a heavy enough shock , things fall apart @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . We can respond to them only by quickly reducing emissions without the benefit of authoritative calculation of cost and benefit . <p> Weather risk in one place is insurable if it is not positively correlated with risk in others ; or if one outcome is damaging for some firms and advantageous for others ; or if one firm is in a better position to absorb bad outcomes than others . <p> Trade in weather derivatives and other forms of insurance can reduce the risk faced by individual firms in places facing independent probability distributions ; or between firms which win and those which lose from unusually hot or wet weather ; or between firms that can absorb climate damage more and less easily . <p> Australia 's unusually variable weather , made more variable with climate change , increases @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with weather patterns correlated only weakly if at all with Australia provides large gains from trade in weather risk . <p> In the energy sector , Australia 's need for and the northern economies ' opportunities for trade in weather-related derivatives and other insurance products will expand as Australian production and export of renewable energy generation for zero-carbon goods increases -- as Australia utilises its opportunity to be the energy superpower of the low carbon world economy . <p> Trade in risk products is of limited value when an adverse event is likely to have similar effects at a similar time over large parts of the world . @@122654793 <h> This month 's High Court ruling on Indigenous property rights confirms the full humanity of First Nations people . By Marcia Langton . <h> The Yunupingu case and native title <p> In the Yunupingu case , handed down by the High Court this month , a rare justice has been delivered . The Yol ? u people have been central to developments in Australian common law in at least two remarkable cases . <p> In the first case -- Milirrpum v Nabalco Pty Ltd , heard by the Supreme Court of the Northern Territory in 1971 -- the rejection of their claim for recognition of their laws on the grounds of the ceded colony argument created the conditions that led to Mabo ( No. ? 2 ) . In this case , the pre-existing laws of Indigenous traditional owners were deemed to be recognised by Australian laws . <p> In the second case -- Commonwealth of Australia v Yunupingu , handed down by the High Court last week -- the Yol ? u people demonstrated that Aboriginal property rights existed and were held to be compensable , at least @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " -- property that is enduring , substantial and significant . <p> The court went further and found that Yol ? u property governed by their laws should be treated equally with all other property under our Constitution and acquired by the Commonwealth only on just terms . The court found the Commonwealth invalidly acquired their rights in a long history of unjust dispossession and that section 122 of the Constitution does not give the Commonwealth power to acquire property other than on just terms . <p> The Gumatj clan is entitled to compensation by the Commonwealth in respect of grants of interests that had the effect of diminishing the Gumatj clan 's pre-existing property rights . Just how much will be determined by another court . <p> Aboriginal people like me have witnessed just how fragile the principle of equality is in Australia , and how subject to many false arguments . <p> The court found that a pastoral lease granted in 1903 by the governor of South Australia did not extinguish any non-exclusive native title rights over minerals on or under the subject land . The future implications @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rights include rights over minerals on or under their land -- is exciting the governments of Australia and the mining industry . <p> There has been no frenzied response , such as the response to Mabo ( No. ? 2 ) in 1992 , but there will be a response to the findings on the Aboriginal right to compensation and their newly recognised mineral rights . It is likely that the response will be one that poses an existential threat to the common law and civil rights of Aboriginal people . <p> The late head of the Gumatj clan of the Yol ? u people , Galarrwuy Yunupingu , instructed his lawyer to litigate for compensation in 2019 . He died in 2023 before he could be vindicated by the remarkable findings of the High Court , but he did at least live to see the favourable findings of the Federal Court in this matter . The Commonwealth appealed unsuccessfully . <p> Yunupingu was present as a young man when his elders discussed the unjust acquisition of their land for mining by the Commonwealth . Under the instruction of his @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ his elders and was appointed as translator in the Milirrpum case . <p> That injustice was a driving force throughout his life . He was determined to overcome the legality of the theft of land , desecration of sacred sites and the damage to Yol ? u society and culture that the mining operations , mining town and company staff inflicted . More than half a century later , the Yol ? u case has been fully vindicated . <p> Just before Christmas in 1962 , the historian Clare Wright recounts , Daympalibu Munu ? gurr , a member of the Djapu clan living at the Methodist mission at Yirrkala , in north-east Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory , came across " a long , neat row of white survey markers bifurcating the mission 's peanut paddock " . At that time , he and other clan leaders did not know the Commonwealth had assumed ownership of all their land estates and had started issuing mining leases . The first , over 21 square miles ( 54 square kilometres ) next to the Methodist mission , was given to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 1958 . <p> Only a few missionaries knew why mining company staff were staking out their land . By 1963 , the scale of the incursion and intentions of the company had become apparent . The clan leaders of the region had a plan . They had convened meetings and wrote a petition to the parliament in one of the languages of the Yol ? u Matha-speaking peoples to protest against the federal government 's decision to allow bauxite mining on their lands . <p> The clans painted sacred designs on bark on which to place the petitions . Two of the four Yirrkala Bark Petitions were presented to parliament on August 14 and August 28 , 1963 , and they remain on display in a cabinet there . <p> They were the first petitions presented to the Australian parliament in an Australian language . They were and remain iconic representations of the conflict between Aboriginal people and mining companies supported by the state to confiscate their land . Such conflict has become a defining feature of the nation , addressed repeatedly by the courts . <p> In 1964 , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ u land for mining with now predictable findings . Not satisfied with the outcome , the elders instructed the lawyer Edward Woodward to act on their behalf in the Supreme Court of the Northern Territory . <p> In 1971 , Justice Richard Blackburn found against the Yol ? u in Milirrpum v Nabalco Pty Ltd , ruling that while there was clear evidence they had their own laws that gave them entitlement under their traditions to the land , these could not be recognised by Australian law . He invoked the " ceded colony " thesis in an Australian version of Sir William Blackstone 's treatise on terra nullius . <p> To overcome the injustice of the Blackburn decision , the Commonwealth turned to Woodward to make recommendations on land rights . In 1976 , the federal parliament enacted the Aboriginal Land Rights ( Northern Territory ) Act 1976 to provide inalienable freehold title to Aboriginal land trusts over former Aboriginal reserves and other lands . <p> Only in the Northern Territory were inherent and pre-existing Aboriginal rights in land recognised , but only by the " grace and favour @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Elsewhere , such rights were largely denied , except in a fragmented and substandard way . <p> In 1992 , in the Mabo ( No. 2 ) case , the " central basis for recognition of native title " was the rejection of terra nullius . In his lead judgement , Justice Gerard Brennan wrote that to continue to recognise the findings of those earlier cases would destroy the equality of all Australian citizens . " The common law of this country would perpetuate injustice if it were to continue to embrace the enlarged notion of terra nullius and to persist in characterising the indigenous inhabitants of the Australian colonies as people too low in the scale of social organization to be acknowledged as possessing rights and interests in land . " <p> In the recent Yunupingu case , the judges relied on several arguments about the import of common law recognition of native title , and particularly the rejection of terra nullius . They refused to perpetuate this " injustice based on an historical fiction " . <p> The judges rejected the Commonwealth argument about the " inherent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and instead preserved the " rationale of equality before the law " because not to do so would " destroy that equality and perpetuate its own form of injustice " . <p> Since 1823 , common law has held that Indigenous people must be considered as " people in possession of a place " . This principle of common law was ignored or denied by Justice Richard Blackburn and its implications were ignored in the statutory codification of native title law -- and in subsequent legal findings of the courts . <p> The decision in Yunupingu is a reminder of the Marshall decision in 1823 in Virginia . The findings in relation to the recognition of Yol ? u property as a " species of property " accords it the same status as the sacred fee simple -- a form of freehold that grants its owner full and complete rights . This finding overcomes three decades of native title dealings that have diminished the common law recognition of native title and have relegated it to a " bundle of rights " and an " inherently fragile " title -- a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ type of property attracting the protection of the constitutional right to just terms compensation for compulsory acquisition . <p> This longstanding view in North American law -- that the Native American right of occupancy is considered as sacred as the fee simple of whites -- is one that only now has been expressed in Australia . In the Marshall decision it was held that indigenous people could not sell their land to settlers . The government , as a successor to the European powers that " discovered " the land , had the sole right to purchase land from Native Americans . Chief Justice John Marshall confirmed the " doctrine of discovery " first promulgated by Pope Alexander VI . Marshall held that " the principle of discovery gave European nations an absolute right to New World lands " . In essence , Native Americans had only a right of occupancy , which could be abolished . This was the " ultimate dominion " of the colonising power . <p> From there , however , Marshall narrowed the legal issues to be considered and found that they were legally in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , which has been called " domestic dependent sovereignty " . This aspect is fundamental to the Native American treaties and their federal status . <p> In particular , Marshall found : " They were admitted to be the rightful occupants of the soil , with a legal as well as just claim to retain possession of it , and to use it to their own discretion ; but their rights to complete sovereignty , as independent nations , were necessarily diminished , and their power to dispose of the soil at their own will , to whomsoever they pleased , was denied by the original fundamental principle that discovery gave exclusive title to those who made it . " <p> Will justice prevail after the Yunupingu case ? <p> Whereas I had once expected a commitment from Australians to the principle of equality before the law , the campaign against the Voice referendum , led by Peter Dutton , has placed this in doubt . <p> The right to just treatment under our Constitution , parliaments and courts can be easily swept aside , more so now than in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ just how fragile the principle of equality is in Australia , and how subject to many false arguments . <p> Respect for the law and the principle of the rule of law are first to be sacrificed when the conflict between Aboriginal people and government or corporate wealth extraction from our land is heightened . This repeated outcome in the history of the nation will put the trust in the courts and the law at risk should another campaign against us begin following the Yunupingu case . <p> In the courts , we had considerable success in establishing our rights . For a brief time -- as I expect it will be brief -- I am appreciating the High Court 's confirmation of our full humanity in finding that the traditional property rights of the Yol ? u are indeed a " species of property " , as sacred as the fee simple of the whites , and that this right is " substantial and significant " . <p> Of great significance , too , is the question that is raised by Marshall in relation to the validity of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ colonised indigenous people . <p> It is conceivable to challenge this , just as Galarrwuy Yunupingu and his elders challenged the theft of their land for more than 70 years , eventually winning their basic claim to be " the rightful occupants of the soil , with a legal as well as just claim to retain possession of it " . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on March 22 , 2025 as " The Yunupingu case " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . All of them should be . <p> I should make some declarations of interest . <p> The major hegemonic parties have become authoritarian , secretive and faction-ridden . @@122654796 <h> Exclusive : Leaked report shows warnings over ' Black robodebt ' <p> A leaked 2024 auditor-general preparation paper , obtained by The Saturday Paper , reveals that successive government ministers and senior bureaucrats were repeatedly advised that the Community Development Program was likely unlawful but did not stop it . <p> The Australian Government Solicitor first provided legal advice in 2015 , stating there was a " medium " to " high " risk the proposed welfare program would breach the Racial Discrimination Act . <p> Over the ensuing six years , the legal advice continued as the Coalition government doubled down on its ideological war on poverty through the punitive remote jobs scheme . <p> The extensive timeline and detailed nature of the legal advice , outlined in the leaked documents , was ultimately removed from the auditor-general 's final report . <p> As one example : where the preparation report said the prime minister 's department sought advice from the Australian Government Solicitor in February 2018 regarding " the risks of direct and indirect racial discrimination " , the final report says the advice was simply " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " . <p> A spokesperson for the audit office said preparation paper did not represent the auditor-general 's final opinion . " The Auditor-General considers the nature of all material and forms an opinion as to what information should be included in a public report to support the audit findings and conclusion . By their nature , Report Preparation Papers will always include more detail than the final report . " <p> In 2021 then Indigenous affairs minister Ken Wyatt received separate advice of a " risk " that the chief executive of the National Indigenous Australians Agency , as well as the secretary of the Department of Education , Skills and Employment , and respective ministers , " may be personally liable for the tort of misfeasance in public office " . Wyatt did not respond to requests for comment . <p> The source who leaked the documents says the program amounted to " Black robodebt " . They said the implementation and administration of the Community Development Program was " the same scale as robodebt ... but for Aboriginal people " . <p> " It was the same @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ same level of devastation to vulnerable people in our community . " <p> Alongside the privatised version of the cashless debit card , the CDP was born out of Andrew Forrest 's 2014 " Creating Parity " report -- also known as the Forrest Review . <p> " The notion that it was robodebt for Blackfellas , I find offensive , quite frankly . I do n't accept the proposition ... I just do n't . I 'm not saying it was the best policy in the world , but there is no way that it was robodebt for Blackfellas . " <p> The Forrest Review was commissioned by then prime minister Tony Abbott and closely supported by then parliamentary secretary Alan Tudge and minister for Indigenous affairs Nigel Scullion . <p> In July 2015 , it was signed into law through the Social Security Act , when Scott Morrison was social services minister . Forrest did not respond to a request for comment . <p> Jon Altman , a social scientist at the Australian National University , said at the time the Forrest review was " the most unsatisfactory @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ years of working in this space " . <p> Today , a rueful Altman says the CDP has " predictably escalated the misery " . <p> " Punishing the poor . Punishing the Black . Punishing the remote . Punishing the relatively powerless , " he says . " And to what end ? " <p> The CDP implemented a regime of mutual obligations and work-for-the-dole schemes in remote communities . Although it was claimed not to be exclusively for Indigenous people , 86 per cent of participants in 2023 were Indigenous . The program was introduced by the then Indigenous affairs minister and is ultimately administered by the National Indigenous Australians Agency . <p> Under the scheme , remote Indigenous people were offered a simple choice : find a job in places where there often were none or indefinitely do work for the dole five hours a day , five days a week , 46 weeks a year , year after year , with the majority of income then managed though the cashless debit card . <p> Remarkably , this was better than the full-time option of 35 hours @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ weeks a year initially announced by the minister , Nigel Scullion . Still , the work requirement of 1150 hours a year was almost double the mainstream jobactive program of 650 hours . <p> Participants were forced to work for an hourly rate of $11.20 , well below the minimum wage of $18.29 . Had Forrest got his way , the hourly rate would have been $7.80 . <p> When participants withdrew their labour , their income support was withdrawn under a " no work , no pay " mantra . <p> A 2017 analysis from the Australian National University showed that the CDP saw a 740 per cent increase in financial penalties , with remote workers 25 times more likely to be penalised than non-remote workers and 55 times more likely to have a serious penalty imposed , which meant up to eight weeks with no payment . <p> A separate Senate inquiry in the same year heard that more than 200,000 breach notices had been issued in the CDP 's first two years . <p> Vanessa Thomas , from the remote community of Mulga Queen in Western Australia @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the inquiry . She described having to travel more than 500 kilometres to reach Kalgoorlie for a medical appointment , only to be breached by the local CDP provider because she did n't show up for work . <p> One year after the Australian Government Solicitor first provided legal advice to the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet about the risk of the then proposed CDP breaching the Racial Discrimination Act , the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights noted in its Human Rights Security Report that " where a measure impacts on a particular group disproportionately , it establishes prima facie that there may be indirect discrimination " . <p> " In CDP 's case it seems clear that Indigenous people will be disproportionately affected by this measure as more than 80 per cent of the people currently supported by CDP providers are Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people . " <p> According to the documents , in December 2016 the Australian Human Rights Commission advised the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet of a complaint made by the remote Western Australian shire of Ngaanyatjarraku , alleging @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2017 , the AGS advised Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet that " the Commonwealth only has moderate prospects of defending the element of indirect discrimination without further evidence " . <p> In the same year , the Senate inquiry recommended " the Australian Government immediately replace the current CDP compliance and penalty regime with obligations that are no more onerous than those of other income support recipients . CDP participants must have the same legal rights and other responsibilities as other income support participants , taking into account special circumstances such as remote locations and cultural obligations " . <p> The government 's response to the recommendation was unequivocal : " The Australian Government does not support this recommendation . " <p> It was a remarkable response , considering the Commonwealth released its own report into the CDP merely four months later , which found that , since its introduction , there was an increase in break and enters to steal food , predominately by children and young people ; an increase in domestic and family violence ; an increase in financial coercion and family fighting ; and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , depression , sleep deprivation and hunger . <p> The report also said CDP participants went without income for longer periods and were less likely to be exempted on medical grounds " despite a much higher burden of disease in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities " . <p> In May 2019 , the mediation to resolve the complaint brought by the Shire of Ngaanyatjarraku was deemed unsuccessful and ultimately terminated by the Australian Human Rights Commission . <p> In July 2019 , Dawson and Ors v Commonwealth of Australia began . <p> Meanwhile , the National Indigenous Australians Agency continued to publicly insist that the CDP complied with the Racial Discrimination Act . <p> According to the leaked documents , however , in September 2020 , in anticipation of the class action court hearing scheduled for February 2021 , the AGS provided advice on the program to the government 's insurance fund , Comcover , the National Indigenous Australians Agency , the Department of Education , Skills and Employment , Services Australia and the Department of Social Services . By Daniel Herborn . <h> Comedian Lou Wall <p> Just moments into a Zoom call with comedian and theatre maker Lou Wall , I 'm plunged into second-hand anxiety . Apparently a clumsy type , they 've spilt water on their laptop and it 's no longer working properly . <p> The thought of anyone losing unsaved work seems like a peculiarly modern hell . In Wall 's case , however , it feels particularly galling as their live comedy shows have an audiovisual backbone , with each hour containing hundreds of sound cues , photos and video clips . " <p> The prospect of their laptop not working and an AV extravaganza suddenly becoming a bare-bones show does n't faze Wall . Things have gone wrong before . Projectors , it turns out , are a common culprit . " They 're like the printers of the art world . Nobody understands them . We can go to the moon , but God forbid I use a HDMI cable . " <p> When the technology fails , Wall has to throw out their meticulously planned collage and instead do an improvised show , talking to the audience to create a one-off performance . " I find a lot of joy in the fuck-ups . For me , the beauty of live art is that you are right there in the moment and there 's nothing that puts me in the moment more than a tech fuck-up . By Naomi Stead . <h> Th ? o Mercier 's Mirrorscape sand sculpture at Mona <p> I 've often felt it 's the sandstone escarpment that steals the show at the Museum of Old and New Art ( Mona ) . Sure , there 's the amazing collection , but the real star is the exposed bedrock in which the museum is embedded : the walls of its tunnels and cavernous main chamber striated by veins and scrabbled by the teeth of machines . It 's powerful stuff : a building both raw and elemental , hewn from a living porous solid that continues to leach salt and seep moisture , to crumble and sprout a creeping stain of green . It 's a netherworld of rich , seamy sandstone . <p> When Mona opened in 2011 , architecture critics greeted it with something like ecstasy . They dug it all : the rock clamps in their niches ; the counterpoint between the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ labyrinthine circulation tangling a stately museum enfilade into a confounding knot ; the way architects Fender Katsalidis refused a coherent form from the outside , instead mining away beneath Roy Grounds ' Courtyard House of 1957 and his Round House of 1958 . The latter , formerly Mona 's library , now houses a major new installation by French artist Th ? o Mercier : Mirrorscape . <p> Mercier , often described as an enfant terrible in the French cultural scene , is as prolific as he is unpindownable . Combining the roles of sculptor and director , he credits an early apprenticeship with Matthew Barney for expanding his practice into world-making . Mercier works with a large creative production team -- something " between a studio and a theatre company " -- which for Mirrorscape includes a posse of sand-compactors and sculptors . <p> If this is a sandcastle , it 's like none you 've ever seen . A head-high bank of pale sand , isolated behind full-height glass , is carved into a jumble of objects and detritus : an overturned car tangled with mattresses and rubber @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and clothing , a capsized handbasin , household appliances , crumpled metal and plastic pipe . All meticulously crafted in sand , it seems the smashed wreckage of some cataclysmic event . <p> The most interesting thing about Mirrorscape is not its form but the process of its un-forming , its gradual and inevitable descent back into loose material . <p> Mercier has elsewhere referred to an earlier sand work as a " diorama of catastrophe " -- another as a " disaster vivarium " . Mirrorscape has the same unsettling quality -- an enclosed world staged for our scrutiny . Museum dioramas , hokey and obsolete as they may be , offer the pleasure of intricate detail , often at miniature scale , enabling a god's-eye view thick with inferred narrative . <p> Mirrorscape shares these qualities but with a markedly more clinical tone . No painted trompe l'oeil scenery , just a stark backdrop of brushed aluminium and a cool , flat overhead lighting array straight out of Severance . It 's less like a narrative scene than a forensic lab , underscored by the shallow curve of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a spectacle laid bare . <p> This mode of work -- remaking matter into the semblance of other matter -- can be a one-liner , despite its evident labour and skill . Contemporary art might be having its " is it cake ? " moment : wow that really looks like a mattress but gee whiz it 's made of sand . Do n't get me wrong , it 's undeniably visually fascinating -- the eye devours its intricacies -- and Mirrorscape is more clever and interesting than pure mimesis . But there 's also something troubling here . <p> The press material breezily asserts that the work is not disaster voyeurism , nor does it aestheticise catastrophe . I 'm not so sure : I sense damage control . Mirrorscape was earlier announced under a different title , " Dark Tourism " , which was changed late and abruptly , presumably when someone realised it was all a bit too close to the bone . We all feel the imminence of catastrophe daily now : the loss of everything you love breathes just behind your ear . This is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to be enjoyed . Mirrorscape veers uncomfortably close to ruin porn . <p> Of course a play on negative aesthetics has always been a useful vehicle for sophisticates : the chance to flaunt their refined sensibilities , their capacity to draw distinctions between repulsive subjects and artful execution . Mona 's nemesis is n't scandal -- it 's boredom . But in a world teeming with real horrors , the museum 's once-subversive shock tactics begin to feel tired , decadent , even self-parodic . <p> The most interesting thing about Mirrorscape is not its form but the process of its un-forming , its gradual and inevitable descent back into loose material . What holds sand together is moisture , specifically the surface tension of water droplets forming tiny bonds between each grain . Too wet , the tension dissipates and it melts into slop . Too dry , the links evaporate and the whole falls into individual particles . As every seaside builder knows , there 's a fragile state of balance between moisture and granularity that will , briefly , hold the artifice together . Sand rises into @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ now Mirrorscape is damp -- its edges crisp , its details sharp . It will soon begin to dry out and crumble : a gradual erasure of detail , a blunting of form , a return to the angle of repose . It questions whether the most profound capacity of art is not the ability to create form from inchoate matter but rather to let it fall away , to see it disintegrate and devolve , to close the circle and return to formlessness . This work reminds us that sand is a crucial component of all modern cities -- as an essential ingredient in concrete . It 's also an extracted resource , which is finite and increasingly scarce . <p> Back at the window , peering in at Mirrorscape , a close observer will notice in the sandy wheel well of the upturned car an emerging , embedded outcrop of natural weathered sandstone . Cold upwellings and deeper currents have soothed the fever of the outer reef , but corals closer to land are stressed , dead or dying . When the water 's too warm -- as it is now at 29.7 degrees at Lizard Island -- the algae within the coral polyps spew highly reactive oxygen molecules that act like tiny bombs to healthy proteins . That triggers the polyps to vomit the algae ; the corals ' source of photosynthetic energy and colour . If conditions do n't cool quickly , the corals die .
